objects.name: Mule Account Velocity Pattern
objects.description: Detects rapid inbound transfers from multiple unique senders followed by immediate outbound movement, typical of money mule activity. This rule is a shared component applicable to TP-0001, TP-0002, TP-0011, and TP-0022.

objects.name: Infostealer Credential Dump Velocity
objects.description: Detects rapid credential dump patterns where many unique credentials are harvested from a single host in a short timeframe. Infostealers such as RedLine, Lumma, and Vidar typically exfiltrate dozens to hundreds of stored credentials within seconds of execution, producing a burst of credential-access events from one endpoint.

objects.name: Session Cookie Exfiltration Pattern
objects.description: Detects session token and cookie theft patterns in log data indicative of infostealer activity. Stealers like Lumma and Raccoon target browser cookie stores to extract active session tokens, enabling session hijacking without requiring credentials. This rule monitors for suspicious access to cookie databases and exfiltration of session-bearing data.

objects.name: Browser Credential Store Access
objects.description: Detects unusual access to browser credential stores (Login Data, logins.json, key3.db/key4.db) by non-browser processes. Infostealers such as RedLine and Vidar systematically read these SQLite databases to extract saved usernames and passwords for banking portals and other financial services.

objects.name: Stealer C2 Beacon Pattern
objects.description: Detects command-and-control callback patterns typical of Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) stealers. RedLine, Lumma, and StealC use distinctive C2 communication patterns including HTTP POST requests with base64-encoded payloads to newly registered domains, often on non-standard ports or with characteristic URI patterns.

objects.name: Credential Testing After Dump
objects.description: Detects rapid credential validation attempts occurring shortly after a credential dump event. After infostealers exfiltrate harvested credentials, threat actors typically run automated validation to identify which stolen credentials are still active, producing a burst of login attempts across multiple banking portals from the attacker's infrastructure.

objects.name: Infostealer Exfiltration Archive Creation
objects.description: Detects creation of archive files containing credential-related file patterns consistent with infostealer packaging behavior. Stealers like RedLine and Vidar collect credentials, cookies, autofill data, and crypto wallet files into a ZIP or RAR archive before exfiltrating them to the C2 server.

objects.name: Multiple Account Access from Single Source
objects.description: Detects multiple distinct banking accounts being accessed from a single device or IP address within a short timeframe. This pattern is consistent with an attacker using stolen credentials from an infostealer dump to sequentially access compromised accounts for reconnaissance or initial positioning before fraudulent transactions.

objects.name: Stolen Session Token Replay
objects.description: Detects session token replay from a different geographic location or device than the original authenticating session. When infostealers exfiltrate active session cookies, attackers import them into antidetect browsers to hijack authenticated sessions without triggering login-based detections. This rule correlates session token usage across differing geolocations and device fingerprints.

objects.name: Autofill Data Harvesting
objects.description: Detects form autofill data extraction patterns consistent with infostealer behavior. Stealers like RedLine and Raccoon target browser autofill databases (Web Data, formhistory.sqlite) to harvest stored PII including names, addresses, phone numbers, and payment card details that facilitate downstream fraud.

objects.name: Crypto Wallet Seed Phrase Exfiltration
objects.description: Detects wallet seed phrase and private key extraction attempts targeting cryptocurrency wallets. Infostealers such as RedLine, Vidar, and StealC include dedicated modules that search for wallet.dat files, seed phrase backups, and keystore directories for MetaMask, Exodus, Electrum, and other popular wallets to enable cryptocurrency theft.

objects.name: Login Velocity Anomaly
objects.description: Detects abnormal login attempt velocity from a single source IP or subnet, indicative of automated credential stuffing tools. Legitimate users produce low single-digit login attempts per minute; credential stuffing tools generate dozens to hundreds, often targeting the authentication API directly rather than the web login form.

objects.name: Geographic Impossibility Login
objects.description: Detects login attempts from geographically impossible locations within a short timeframe. When a user authenticates from one country and a second authentication occurs from a distant country within a window that makes physical travel impossible, it strongly indicates credential compromise and concurrent use by an attacker.

objects.name: Device Fingerprint Anomaly
objects.description: Detects a known device fingerprint presenting with changed underlying characteristics such as OS version, screen resolution, timezone, or installed fonts. Attackers using antidetect browsers (Multilogin, GoLogin, Dolphin Anty) import stolen device fingerprints but often have mismatches in lower-level hardware attributes that this rule correlates.

objects.name: Combo List Iteration Pattern
objects.description: Detects sequential username patterns typical of combo list iteration during credential stuffing attacks. Attackers feed sorted credential lists into stuffing tools, producing login attempts where usernames appear in alphabetical or near-alphabetical order with minimal timing variation between attempts, a pattern never seen in organic user behavior.

objects.name: Distributed Credential Stuffing
objects.description: Detects low-and-slow distributed credential stuffing attacks spread across multiple source IPs to evade per-IP rate limiting. Advanced attackers use residential proxy networks and botnets to distribute attempts, making each source IP appear benign while the aggregate attack targets many accounts. This rule aggregates failed login patterns across source IPs sharing common characteristics.

objects.name: Residential Proxy Login Attempt
objects.description: Detects login attempts originating from known residential proxy networks. Credential stuffing actors increasingly route attacks through residential proxies (Luminati/Bright Data, Oxylabs, SmartProxy) to appear as legitimate home users and bypass IP-reputation blocklists. This rule correlates source IPs against residential proxy threat intelligence feeds.

objects.name: Credential Spray Single Password
objects.description: Detects password spraying attacks where a single password (or small set of passwords) is tested across many accounts. Unlike traditional credential stuffing which uses unique username-password pairs, password spraying tries common or recently breached passwords against a large account population to avoid per-account lockout thresholds.

objects.name: Beneficiary Change Velocity Anomaly
objects.description: Detects multiple beneficiary additions or modifications on a single account within a short time window. Rapid beneficiary changes are a strong pre-cursor to payment diversion fraud, where an attacker positions new destination accounts before initiating unauthorized wires.

objects.name: Rapid Contact Information Change
objects.description: Detects when email, phone number, and mailing address are all changed on an account within a short window. A full contact information swap is a hallmark of account takeover where the attacker locks out the legitimate owner before executing fraud.

objects.name: MFA Method Switch Before High-Value Transaction
objects.description: Detects when an account's multi-factor authentication method is changed (e.g., from hardware token to SMS or email OTP) shortly before a high-value wire or ACH transaction is initiated. Attackers downgrade MFA to a method they control prior to executing fraud.

objects.name: Dormant Account Reactivation
objects.description: Detects accounts with no transactional activity for 90 or more days that suddenly initiate financial transactions. Dormant accounts are frequently targeted by attackers because they are less likely to be monitored and credential compromise may go unnoticed.

objects.name: Alert Threshold Modification
objects.description: Detects when a user modifies their own transaction alert thresholds or disables notifications via online banking or mobile app. Attackers raise alert thresholds or suppress notifications to prevent the legitimate account holder from being alerted to unauthorized transactions.

objects.name: Wire Beneficiary Name Mismatch
objects.description: Detects when the wire beneficiary name provided by the originator does not match the account holder name at the receiving institution. Name mismatches on wire transfers are a strong indicator of payment diversion fraud where funds are redirected to accounts controlled by the attacker.

objects.name: Power of Attorney or Authorized Signer Change
objects.description: Detects changes to power of attorney designations or authorized signers on commercial and business accounts. Fraudsters may socially engineer or forge POA documents to gain control of business accounts, enabling them to initiate high-value transactions.

objects.name: Account Type Conversion Anomaly
objects.description: Detects suspicious account type conversions such as savings-to-checking or personal-to-business. These conversions can unlock higher transaction limits, wire capabilities, or ACH origination, which attackers exploit to move larger amounts after taking over a limited account.

objects.name: First-Time International Wire to New Country
objects.description: Detects international wire transfers sent to a country that has no prior transaction history for the originating account. First-time international wires, especially to high-risk corridors, are a key indicator of business email compromise and payment diversion schemes.

objects.name: Transaction Amount Clustering Near Reporting Threshold
objects.description: Detects transactions that cluster just below regulatory reporting thresholds ($3,000 for international transfers, $10,000 for CTR filing). Structuring transactions to evade reporting requirements is itself a federal offense and a strong indicator of money laundering or fraud monetization.

objects.name: Split Transfer Chain Detection
objects.description: Detects when a large inbound amount is split into multiple smaller outbound transfers to different beneficiaries in sequence. This layering technique is used to obscure the origin and destination of fraudulently obtained funds.

objects.name: After-Hours Wire Transfer Initiation
objects.description: Detects wire transfers initiated outside the account's established normal business hours. Attackers often execute unauthorized wires during evenings, weekends, or holidays when fraud detection staff and account holders are less likely to notice.

objects.name: Rapid Outbound Wire After Large Inbound
objects.description: Detects a large outbound wire or ACH transfer initiated within hours of receiving a large inbound deposit. This pass-through pattern is characteristic of compromised accounts being used as intermediary conduits in fraud or money laundering schemes.

objects.name: Beneficiary Country Mismatch with Business Profile
objects.description: Detects wire transfers to countries where the account holder has no established business relationship or prior transaction history. Combined with other indicators, this can reveal business email compromise where payment instructions are altered to redirect funds to attacker-controlled accounts in foreign jurisdictions.

objects.name: Round-Dollar Wire Amount Pattern
objects.description: Detects unusual patterns of wire transfers in round dollar amounts (e.g., $5,000, $10,000, $25,000). While individual round-amount wires are common, a pattern of multiple round-amount wires is atypical for legitimate business payments and may indicate structured or test transactions by fraudsters.

objects.name: ACH Return Rate Anomaly
objects.description: Detects ACH originators with an elevated return or reversal rate exceeding normal thresholds. High ACH return rates (especially R10 unauthorized, R29 corporate not authorized) may indicate the account is being used to initiate unauthorized debits against victim accounts.

objects.name: Wire to FATF High-Risk Jurisdiction
objects.description: Detects wire transfers to jurisdictions on the FATF high-risk or increased monitoring lists. While not inherently fraudulent, wires to these jurisdictions combined with other risk factors (new beneficiary, unusual amount, after-hours) significantly elevate the risk of money laundering or fraud monetization.

objects.name: Payment Instruction Velocity Spike
objects.description: Detects when multiple payment instructions (wires, ACH batches, or internal transfers) are submitted in rapid succession from a single account or user session. High-velocity payment submissions suggest automated or scripted fraud execution, often seen after credential compromise.

objects.name: Mule Rapid ATM Withdrawal After Inbound Transfer
objects.description: Detects cash withdrawals at ATMs occurring shortly after an inbound wire or ACH transfer. Money mules frequently convert electronically received fraud proceeds to cash as quickly as possible to prevent recovery, often hitting daily ATM limits across multiple machines.

objects.name: Account Age vs Transaction Volume Mismatch
objects.description: Detects accounts less than 90 days old that exhibit transaction volumes exceeding the typical profile for mature accounts. Newly opened accounts with abnormally high volume are a primary indicator of purpose-built mule accounts created specifically to funnel illicit funds.

objects.name: Multi-Bank Funnel Pattern
objects.description: Detects accounts receiving funds from multiple external financial institutions that are then consolidated and sent outbound to a single destination. This funnel pattern is a hallmark of money mule operations where proceeds from multiple fraud victims are aggregated before being laundered.

objects.name: Crypto Off-Ramp After Wire or ACH Receipt
objects.description: Detects a pattern where an account receives a wire or ACH credit and then promptly initiates a transfer to a known cryptocurrency exchange or digital asset platform. Converting fraud proceeds to cryptocurrency provides near-irreversible laundering, making this a critical monetization indicator.

objects.name: Peer-to-Peer Transfer Chain (Smurfing Pattern)
objects.description: Detects chains of peer-to-peer transfers across multiple accounts where funds move through a sequence of intermediary accounts (A to B to C to D). This smurfing pattern is used to layer fraud proceeds through multiple hops, making tracing difficult.

objects.name: Mule Recruitment Test Deposit Pattern
objects.description: Detects accounts receiving multiple small "test" deposits from many distinct external sources. Mule recruiters validate new mule accounts by sending micro-deposits from various fraud proceeds before routing larger amounts. The pattern of many small inbound transfers from unrelated senders is highly anomalous for personal accounts.

objects.name: Rapid Fund Layering Through Shell Accounts
objects.description: Detects rapid fund movement through multiple accounts with minimal retention time, indicative of layering through shell or pass-through accounts. Funds transit through each account within hours with near-zero balance retention, suggesting the accounts exist solely to obscure the money trail.

objects.name: Carrier Change Authentication Correlation
objects.description: Detects a carrier or SIM change event immediately followed by an authentication attempt on a banking platform. SIM swap attacks involve social engineering or insider compromise at a mobile carrier to port the victim's phone number to an attacker-controlled SIM, after which the attacker uses SMS-based MFA to access accounts. The tight temporal correlation between carrier change and login is the key indicator.

objects.name: New Device High-Value Transaction
objects.description: Detects a high-value financial transaction initiated from a new or previously unknown device shortly after initial authentication. Attackers who have compromised credentials and bypassed MFA via SIM swap typically move quickly to execute high-value transfers from a device with no prior history on the account, exploiting the narrow window before the victim notices.

objects.name: MFA Push Bombing
objects.description: Detects rapid repeated MFA push notifications sent to the same user, a technique known as MFA fatigue or push bombing. Attackers who have obtained valid credentials bombard the victim with push authentication requests, hoping the user will approve one out of frustration or confusion, thereby granting the attacker access.

objects.name: SIM Swap Indicator Chain
objects.description: Detects the full SIM swap attack chain: phone number change followed by password reset followed by high-value account action in rapid sequence. This multi-stage correlation captures the complete attack lifecycle where the attacker first takes over the phone number, then uses it to reset the account password via SMS OTP, and finally executes a high-value transfer or account modification.

objects.name: VoIP Number MFA Enrollment
objects.description: Detects MFA enrollment using VoIP or virtual phone numbers instead of legitimate mobile carrier numbers. Attackers who have compromised an account often enroll a disposable VoIP number (Google Voice, TextNow, Twilio) as the MFA phone to maintain persistent access and intercept future OTP codes without relying on SIM swap persistence.

objects.name: MFA Method Downgrade
objects.description: Detects when an account's MFA method is changed from a strong phishing-resistant factor (FIDO2/WebAuthn, hardware token, authenticator app) to a weaker method (SMS OTP, voice call). Attackers who compromise account credentials may downgrade the MFA method to one they can intercept via SIM swap or SS7 exploitation, enabling persistent account takeover.

objects.name: Voice Biometric Confidence Score Anomaly for Known Caller
objects.description: Detects when a voice biometric verification score for a previously enrolled caller falls below an acceptable confidence threshold, which may indicate a deepfake or voice-clone attempt impersonating a legitimate customer. Legitimate callers typically produce scores above 85; scores between 40-70 with a previously stable voiceprint warrant investigation.

objects.name: Callback Number Mismatch for Claimed Institution
objects.description: Detects when an inbound caller claims to represent a specific financial institution or internal department, but the originating ANI or callback number does not match the institution's known directory of outbound numbers. This is a common indicator of vishing and social engineering, especially when combined with voice-clone technology to impersonate bank officials.

objects.name: Audio Compression Artifacts Indicative of AI-Generated Speech
objects.description: Detects audio streams exhibiting compression artifacts, spectral anomalies, or frequency-band irregularities characteristic of AI-generated or text-to-speech synthesis engines. These include unnaturally uniform pitch contours, missing micro-pauses, absence of breath sounds, and codec artifacts from re-encoding through real-time deepfake pipelines.

objects.name: Deepfake Anomalies in Video KYC Session
objects.description: Detects anomalies during video KYC (Know Your Customer) sessions that may indicate the use of deepfake technology. Indicators include irregular frame rates suggesting real-time face-swapping, inconsistent lighting between face and background, lip-sync desynchronization, unnatural eye-blink patterns, and face-boundary artifacts.

objects.name: AI-Generated Document Detection in Verification
objects.description: Detects indicators of AI-generated or synthetically created identity documents submitted during verification workflows. Flags include metadata anomalies (missing EXIF data, uniform noise patterns), font rendering inconsistencies, micro-printing irregularities, and GAN-generated portrait artifacts such as asymmetric earrings or irregular hair boundaries.

objects.name: Real-Time Payment to New Payee After Credential or Contact Change
objects.description: Detects when a real-time or instant payment (Zelle, FedNow, RTP) is initiated to a previously unseen payee within 24 hours of a credential change (password reset, MFA re-enrollment) or contact information update (email, phone, address). This pattern is strongly associated with account takeover followed by immediate monetization via authorized push payment.

objects.name: Instant Payment Velocity Spike Above 30-Day Baseline
objects.description: Detects a sudden spike in instant payment frequency that significantly exceeds the account's established 30-day baseline. A spike is defined as the current day's instant payment count exceeding 3 standard deviations above the rolling 30-day mean, indicating potential account compromise or mule activity where the account is being drained rapidly.

objects.name: Cross-Platform Deposit and Withdrawal Chain
objects.description: Detects a pattern where funds are received via one payment rail (e.g., ACH, wire) and then immediately sent out via a different payment rail (e.g., Zelle, FedNow) within a short window. This cross-rail chaining is a common layering technique used to obscure the origin of funds and complicate tracing, often associated with money mule operations and authorized push payment fraud monetization.

objects.name: Repeated A2A Payments at Maximum Per-Transaction Limit
objects.description: Detects multiple account-to-account payments where each transaction is at or near the maximum per-transaction limit (e.g., $2,500 for Zelle, $500,000 for FedNow). Fraudsters often structure payments at the exact limit to maximize extraction speed while avoiding aggregate-amount alerts, a behavior rarely seen in legitimate consumer transactions.

objects.name: New Account Sending Multiple Instant Payments
objects.description: Detects accounts less than 30 days old that initiate multiple instant payments within a short time window. Newly opened accounts used for rapid instant-payment disbursement are a strong indicator of synthetic identity fraud or mule accounts created specifically for the monetization phase of a fraud scheme.

objects.name: Zelle Recipient Enumeration via Multiple Failed Lookups
objects.description: Detects multiple failed Zelle recipient lookups from a single account or session, which may indicate enumeration activity. Attackers probe email addresses and phone numbers to identify which are registered with Zelle before launching targeted social engineering or authorized push payment attacks against confirmed users.

objects.name: Real-Time Payment Followed by Immediate Refund or Return Request
objects.description: Detects a pattern where a real-time payment (RTP or FedNow) is sent and then an immediate refund, return, or Request for Return of Funds (RROF) is submitted within a short window. This pattern may indicate a double-dip fraud scheme where the sender initiates an irrevocable payment, then exploits the refund process to recover funds while the recipient also retains them.

objects.name: Fake Tracking ID (FTID) Refund Fraud Indicators
objects.description: Detects indicators of fake tracking ID (FTID) refund fraud, where a customer claims a package was not received or returned by providing a manipulated or fabricated tracking number. Indicators include tracking numbers that show delivery to the carrier facility but not to the customer address, tracking IDs associated with lightweight packages inconsistent with the order, or reuse of known FTID patterns across multiple refund claims.

objects.name: Abnormally High Refund Rate Per Customer Account
objects.description: Detects customer accounts with an abnormally high refund-to-order ratio over a rolling window. Accounts exceeding a refund rate of 40% across 10 or more orders within 90 days are flagged as potential refund abusers or participants in refunding-as-a-service (RaaS) schemes, where professional refunders exploit return policies systematically.

objects.name: Triangulation Fraud Shipping Pattern Detection
objects.description: Detects orders where the shipping address differs from the billing address and matches known drop-ship or reshipping patterns associated with triangulation fraud. In triangulation fraud, a fraudster lists goods on a marketplace, collects payment from a victim buyer, then purchases the item from a legitimate retailer using stolen payment credentials, shipping directly to the victim. Indicators include shipping to known drop addresses, freight forwarders, or addresses seen across multiple unrelated accounts.

objects.name: Return Without Receipt Clustering by Customer or Region
objects.description: Detects clusters of product returns submitted without receipts or order references from the same customer identity or geographic region. Organized return fraud rings often exploit no-receipt return policies by using stolen merchandise or purchasing items specifically for return, concentrating activity across nearby store locations or using multiple accounts linked to the same region.

objects.name: High-Value Item Not Received Claims Exceeding Threshold
objects.description: Detects "item not received" (INR) claims filed on high-value orders that exceed a configurable dollar threshold. High-value INR claims are a primary vector for refund fraud, particularly when the delivery confirmation shows successful delivery. Repeated INR claims on expensive items from the same account or device fingerprint are strong indicators of first-party fraud or professional refunding services.

objects.name: Excessive Promotional Code or Coupon Abuse from Related Accounts
objects.description: Detects excessive use of promotional codes, referral bonuses, or coupon offers from accounts that share common attributes such as device fingerprint, IP address, payment method, or shipping address. This pattern indicates promo abuse rings that create multiple accounts to exploit new-customer or referral promotions repeatedly, often using synthetic or stolen identities.

objects.name: DPRK IT Worker Resume Geographic Mismatch
objects.description: Detects job applicants whose resume combines a U.S. residential address with education credentials from non-North American institutions (Singapore, Japan, Hong Kong, China, South Korea). This pattern is a key DPRK IT worker indicator documented by FBI IC3 and DOJ enforcement actions. Legitimate applicants with this profile exist, but the combination with thin credit files or recently created LinkedIn profiles significantly elevates risk.

objects.name: VPN/Proxy Login Anomaly — Astrill or Residential Proxy
objects.description: Detects corporate VPN authentication events originating from known Astrill VPN infrastructure, residential proxy services, or connection patterns indicating VPN-over-VPN layering. DPRK IT workers route connections through Astrill VPN to U.S.-based proxy laptops before connecting to corporate infrastructure, creating a characteristic multi-hop pattern with elevated latency and IP reputation indicators.

objects.name: Multi-Operator Behavioral Shift — Timezone and Communication Anomaly
objects.description: Detects behavioral patterns suggesting multiple operators are sharing a single employee identity. Indicators include login activity spanning incompatible timezones within a single day, significant shifts in communication style or vocabulary between time windows, and device fingerprint changes that correlate with timezone transitions. DPRK IT workers often operate in shifts from different locations using the same stolen identity.

objects.name: Bulk Code Repository Clone by New Employee
objects.description: Detects a new employee (within first 14 days of onboarding) cloning or downloading multiple code repositories, especially repositories outside their assigned team or project scope. DPRK IT workers frequently begin exfiltrating source code within hours of gaining access, cloning entire organizational repositories to personal GitHub accounts or external cloud storage.

objects.name: Credential Store Access Anomaly During Onboarding
objects.description: Detects new employees accessing browser credential stores, password managers, API key management systems, or SSO session token stores at rates significantly above peer baselines during the first 14 days of employment. DPRK IT workers harvest credentials, session cookies, and API keys early in their tenure for exfiltration to DPRK cyber units and as leverage for post-termination extortion.

objects.name: Salary Direct Deposit Rapid Cryptocurrency Conversion
objects.description: Detects patterns where salary direct deposit payments are rapidly converted to cryptocurrency (USDT, USDC, BTC) within 48 hours of deposit, particularly when the receiving account was recently opened or when multiple employee accounts show the same conversion pattern through the same exchange or payment processor. DPRK IT workers convert salary to cryptocurrency for transfer to regime-controlled wallets, often using daily conversion limits to avoid AML alerts.

objects.name: Post-Termination Data Extortion Indicator
objects.description: Detects indicators of post-termination data extortion, where a recently terminated or resigned employee communicates ransom demands referencing specific internal proprietary code, documents, or trade secrets. DPRK IT workers have escalated to this tactic since mid-2024, threatening to publish exfiltrated source code on public repositories or sell proprietary data unless payment is made. Indicators include communication from personal channels containing references to internal systems, and the appearance of company code on public GitHub repositories created by former employee-linked accounts.

objects.name: E-Skimmer Script Injection on Payment Pages
objects.description: Detects unauthorized JavaScript injection on e-commerce payment pages by identifying Content Security Policy violations, unexpected external script loads from newly registered domains, and unauthorized Google Tag Manager container modifications. Magecart-style e-skimmer operators inject malicious scripts through CMS exploitation, compromised third-party libraries, or GTM container abuse. The "Sniffer by Fleras" MaaS platform accounts for 26% of all infections, and GTM container abuse has become a primary delivery vector due to GTM's trusted status in most CSP configurations. PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 6.4.3 mandates automated script integrity monitoring on payment pages, making this detection a compliance requirement as well as a security control.

objects.name: Blockchain C2 and WebSocket Exfiltration from Payment Pages
objects.description: Detects payment page scripts making calls to blockchain RPC endpoints or establishing WebSocket connections to unknown servers, indicating potential e-skimmer data exfiltration via blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure. Advanced Magecart variants observed in 2025 use a loader script on the compromised site that queries a blockchain smart contract (Ethereum, BNB Chain) to retrieve the address of a second-stage payload server, then establishes a WebSocket connection for both payload delivery and data exfiltration. This technique provides censorship-resistant C2 that cannot be disrupted through conventional domain seizure or hosting provider takedown. Detection focuses on identifying JSON-RPC calls to blockchain node endpoints (Infura, Alchemy, direct nodes) and WebSocket connections to non-payment-related servers originating from payment page context.

objects.name: Unauthorized Checkout Page DOM Modification
objects.description: Detects modifications to checkout page DOM elements — including payment form fields, submit buttons, and iframe injections — that occur outside authorized deployment windows or without corresponding change management records. E-skimmer operators manipulate checkout page DOM to inject fake payment form overlays, intercept form submission events, or create invisible iframes that mirror payment forms to capture card data. Legitimate checkout page modifications should only occur during scheduled deployment windows and should be tracked in version control and change management systems. Any DOM mutation on payment form elements that does not correlate with an authorized release is a high-confidence indicator of e-skimmer injection. This rule supports PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 6.4.3 for script and content integrity monitoring on payment pages.

objects.name: Scam Merchant High-Velocity Transaction Pattern
objects.description: Detects merchant accounts exhibiting high initial transaction velocity, elevated chargeback ratios, and short account age — a pattern consistent with purchase scam merchant operations. Recorded Future identified 3,600+ scam merchant accounts in 2025, a 2.5x increase from 2024, operating across 40+ countries and 230+ acquirers. Scam merchants typically process high transaction volumes within their first 30-90 days to extract maximum revenue before chargeback volume triggers acquirer intervention and account termination. Normal new merchant ramp-up is fewer than 50 transactions per day in the first 30 days, ramping to 200+ by day 90. Scam merchants frequently exceed 200 transactions per day within the first two weeks, combined with chargeback rates exceeding 1.5% within 60 days of account opening. This rule also flags merchants with account ages under 90 days that have already accumulated chargeback ratios above scheme monitoring thresholds.

objects.name: Subscription Trap Billing Pattern Detection
objects.description: Detects recurring billing patterns characteristic of subscription trap scam merchants, where initial low-value trial charges are followed by significantly higher recurring charges to merchants with elevated dispute rates. Purchase scam operators enroll victims in subscription billing through obscured terms buried in checkout flows — initial charges are typically under $10 (trial pricing) while subsequent recurring charges escalate to $50-$200+ per cycle. Recorded Future identified this pattern across scam merchant networks in 2025, with some operations adding a secondary "transaction recovery service" charge in H2 2025. Detection focuses on merchants where the ratio of maximum to minimum charge amount exceeds 5:1, recurring billing constitutes more than 30% of transactions, initial charges are below $10, and the merchant has an elevated dispute rate relative to its age and category. Normal subscription merchants show a recurring billing enrollment rate of 5-15% of total transactions, and legitimate trial-to-paid conversions typically maintain a ratio under 3:1.

objects.name: Wallet Provisioning Following OTP Interception Indicator
objects.description: Detects digital wallet provisioning events where the OTP or verification code was delivered within minutes of a social engineering indicator, such as an inbound call from a suspicious source, a phishing link click, or a smishing response. Legitimate wallet provisioning is typically self-initiated, with OTP-to-provisioning intervals of 30-120 seconds. When provisioning occurs within 15 seconds of OTP delivery, or when OTP delivery is preceded by a phishing or social engineering indicator within a 30-minute window, this strongly suggests automated interception-to-provision attack chains associated with digital wallet fraud (TP-0037). The card provisioning attempt is the critical disruption point where refined controls can prevent downstream contactless fraud.

objects.name: NFC Relay Geographic Impossibility on Contactless Transaction
objects.description: Detects contactless (tap-to-pay) transactions where the POS terminal location is geographically impossible given the cardholder's last known location. When a contactless transaction occurs at a POS terminal more than 100 kilometers from the cardholder's most recent authenticated activity (mobile banking login, ATM withdrawal, or prior in-person transaction) within a timeframe that makes physical travel impossible, it indicates NFC relay (ghost-tapping) or unauthorized wallet token use. This rule specifically targets the Phase 4 execution stage of digital wallet fraud and NFC relay attacks (TP-0037), where money mules conduct contactless purchases using relayed card data at POS terminals geographically distant from the legitimate cardholder.

objects.name: Ghost-Tap Multi-Terminal Contactless Velocity Anomaly
objects.description: Detects multiple contactless transactions from the same wallet token or card credential across multiple distinct POS terminals within a short timeframe. Normal cardholder behavior produces a maximum of 2-3 contactless transactions per hour across different terminals during shopping activity. NFC relay (ghost-tapping) operations using tools such as SuperCardX, NFCGate, Hyper NFC, or Valkirie NFC enable simultaneous contactless transactions at multiple POS terminals by relaying stolen card data to multiple money mule devices. This rule detects the Phase 4 execution pattern of TP-0037 where the same wallet token appears at 3 or more distinct POS terminals within 30 minutes, a pattern that is physically impossible for a single cardholder and pathognomonic for NFC relay fraud.

objects.name: Card Testing Micro-Authorization Velocity Spike
objects.description: Detects high velocity of sub-dollar ($0.01-$0.99) authorization attempts from the same merchant or source against multiple distinct card numbers, a pattern characteristic of automated card testing operations. Recorded Future's 2025 report identified over 1,350 tester merchant accounts, with 94% being newly registered merchants. Normal merchant sub-dollar authorization rates are under 0.5% of total authorizations. Card testing operations generate authorization streams where sub-dollar transactions dominate, decline rates exceed 70%, and unique card numbers per source per hour reach 50-500+. This rule targets Phase 4 of TP-0038, detecting the execution of automated card validation at scale through micro-authorization patterns that deviate from legitimate merchant transaction profiles.

objects.name: BIN Enumeration Sequential Card Number Attack
objects.description: Detects sequential or near-sequential card number authorization attempts sharing the same Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefix with incremental variation in the remaining digits. BIN enumeration attacks generate valid card numbers by iterating through possible combinations within a BIN range, validating each against live payment infrastructure through sub-dollar authorization requests. Sequential card numbers from the same BIN prefix have a zero false positive rate for legitimate merchants — this pattern is exclusively associated with fraudulent enumeration. Recorded Future's 2025 report documents BIN attacks as a primary method for generating valid card credentials for downstream fraud, with enumerated cards feeding into card testing (TP-0038), digital wallet provisioning (TP-0037), and card-not-present fraud operations. This rule targets Phase 4 of TP-0038.

objects.name: Agent Intent Manipulation — Purchase Divergence from User Intent
objects.description: Detects transactions initiated by AI agents where the product or service purchased diverges significantly from the user's stated intent or historical purchasing patterns, or where the receiving merchant is flagged as high-risk. This rule targets Phase 3 (Positioning) of agentic commerce fraud, where threat actors manipulate agent purchasing intent to redirect transactions to attacker-controlled merchants or execute purchases that do not reflect the consumer's actual desires. Key indicators include purchases in product categories the user has never engaged with, transactions at merchants created within the last 30 days, transaction amounts exceeding 3x the user's historical average, and merchants with elevated risk scores.

objects.name: Agent Transaction Velocity Anomaly
objects.description: Detects AI agent-initiated transactions at velocities exceeding human purchasing patterns, including multiple purchases per minute and simultaneous multi-merchant purchases within a single agent session. This rule targets Phase 4 (Execution) of agentic commerce fraud, where compromised or manipulated agents execute unauthorized transactions at machine speed. Normal agent purchasing velocity is 1-5 purchases per user session with 2-15 minutes of comparison shopping per purchase. Velocities exceeding 10x human baseline (more than 5 transactions per minute or purchases across more than 3 merchants within a 60-second window) suggest automated fraud exploitation rather than legitimate agent-assisted shopping.

objects.name: BNPL Account Opening Risk Signal Cluster
objects.description: Detects BNPL account applications exhibiting multiple risk signals indicative of synthetic identity fraud. Specifically targets accounts opened with email domains less than 30 days old, minimal digital footprint (score below 0.2), and patterns consistent with emulator-based mass account creation. BNPL providers using soft-check-only approval processes are particularly vulnerable to synthetic identities that pass initial verification but exhibit these digital footprint anomalies. This rule supports detection at Phase 2 of TP-0040 by identifying high-risk onboarding patterns before the synthetic identity progresses to credit grooming and multi-provider stacking.

objects.name: BNPL Multi-Provider Application Velocity
objects.description: Detects identities applying to three or more distinct BNPL providers within a 72-hour window, a pattern characteristic of multi-provider stacking operations. Legitimate consumers rarely apply to more than two BNPL providers within a week. Synthetic identity rings exploit the absence of cross-bureau BNPL loan reporting to accumulate $3,000-$15,000 in aggregate exposure across providers while each provider sees only their individual exposure. This rule requires consortium-level data sharing to be effective, as individual providers cannot detect cross-provider application velocity in isolation. At Phase 3 of TP-0040, multi-provider stacking represents the critical positioning step before coordinated bust-out execution.

objects.name: BNPL Spending Step-Up to Limit Bust-Out Pattern
objects.description: Detects the characteristic spending escalation pattern of BNPL bust-out fraud, where accounts begin with small purchases (under $50) during a credit grooming phase, then rapidly escalate to purchases consuming 85% or more of the available credit limit within 14 days. This pattern distinguishes synthetic bust-out operations from legitimate consumer behavior, where spending typically ramps gradually over weeks to months. Recorded in organized rings deploying 50-1,000+ synthetic identities, the grooming-to-bustout transition represents the highest-confidence detection window for TP-0040 Phase 4 execution, as the sharp behavioral shift from conservative to aggressive spending is difficult for fraudsters to avoid without sacrificing the speed required for coordinated multi-provider bust-out.

objects.name: BNPL Item-Not-Received Claim Velocity
objects.description: Detects accounts filing three or more item-not-received (INR) claims within a 90-day rolling window where the average disputed order value exceeds $300. Legitimate INR dispute rates are under 1% of orders, with most disputes involving genuine delivery failures. Organized phantom delivery fraud and friendly fraud operations systematically file INR claims after receiving goods, targeting high-value orders to maximize returns. This rule supports TP-0040 Phase 4 detection by identifying accounts exhibiting claim patterns consistent with organized INR abuse rather than genuine delivery issues. The $300 average threshold filters out low-value legitimate disputes while capturing the high-value targeting characteristic of organized fraud.

objects.name: BNPL Cross-Account Device Clustering
objects.description: Detects four or more distinct BNPL accounts created from or accessed by the same device fingerprint within a 30-day window, indicating potential synthetic identity ring activity or account farming operations. Normal BNPL usage involves 1-2 accounts per device over 12 months. Emulator-based mass account opening tools with device fingerprint spoofing can create dozens of accounts per day from a single physical device, but sophisticated device fingerprinting systems can detect emulator signatures and fingerprint collision patterns. This rule supports TP-0040 Phase 3 detection by identifying device-level clustering that precedes multi-provider stacking and coordinated bust-out.

objects.name: RDGA Registration Timing Pattern Detection
objects.description: Detects clusters of domain registrations exhibiting algorithmically regular timing intervals in zone file diffs, a hallmark of Registered Domain Generation Algorithm (RDGA) infrastructure provisioning. Legitimate bulk registrations by brand protection services or hosting providers typically show irregular, human-driven timing patterns. RDGA tooling operates programmatically, producing registration bursts with low standard deviation in inter-registration intervals. This rule alerts when a cluster of newly registered domains exceeds a size threshold and the inter-registration timing standard deviation falls below a regularity threshold, indicating automated generation. Supports TP-0041 Phase 2 detection of RDGA-based initial access infrastructure staging.

objects.name: RDGA Nameserver Clustering Anomaly
objects.description: Detects disproportionate concentration of newly registered domains pointing to the same nameserver infrastructure within a 24-hour window. RDGA operators typically provision hundreds or thousands of domains but anchor them to a small set of nameservers they control, creating a fan-in pattern that is statistically anomalous compared to legitimate registrar or hosting provider distributions. Legitimate nameservers serving large numbers of new domains tend to be well-known hosting or registrar nameservers with established reputation. This rule identifies nameserver endpoints receiving an abnormal influx of newly registered domain delegations, filtering out known hosting infrastructure. Supports TP-0041 Phase 2 detection of RDGA nameserver infrastructure consolidation.

objects.name: RDGA Registrar Concentration Anomaly
objects.description: Detects anomalous concentration of new domain registrations at a single registrar that share lexical similarity patterns and nameserver infrastructure, indicating RDGA-driven bulk registration campaigns. Threat actors frequently exploit registrars with weak abuse controls, automated APIs, or low-cost bulk pricing to register large volumes of algorithmically generated domains. This rule correlates three signals: high registration volume at a single registrar, lexical similarity among the registered domain names (e.g., consonant-vowel patterns, character n-gram overlap, or string edit distance clustering), and shared nameserver delegation. The combination of these factors distinguishes RDGA activity from legitimate bulk registration by portfolio investors or brand protection services. Supports TP-0041 Phase 2 detection of registrar abuse for RDGA infrastructure provisioning.

objects.name: TDS Redirect Chain Depth Anomaly
objects.description: Detects HTTP redirect chains (302, 301, or JavaScript-based redirects) exceeding a depth threshold where intermediate nodes are newly registered domains or have low reputation scores, indicating Traffic Distribution System (TDS) abuse. Legitimate web redirects rarely exceed 3 hops and typically traverse well-known CDN, analytics, or marketing infrastructure. TDS chains commonly use 4-7 or more hops through disposable intermediary domains to obfuscate the final destination, evade URL blocklists, and enable real-time traffic steering. Each hop in a TDS chain may perform user-agent filtering, geolocation checks, or bot detection before forwarding. This rule correlates redirect depth with domain age and reputation of intermediate nodes to distinguish malicious TDS chains from legitimate multi-hop redirects. Supports TP-0042 Phase 3 detection of TDS positioning and traffic funneling infrastructure.

objects.name: TDS Cloaking Behavior Detection
objects.description: Detects domains serving divergent content based on visitor attributes such as geolocation, device fingerprint, or user agent, a technique known as cloaking. TDS operators serve benign or empty content to security scanner user agents (e.g., Googlebot, bingbot, crawlers), datacenter IP ranges, and known security vendor IP addresses, while delivering redirects or malicious content to residential IP addresses and consumer device fingerprints. This rule identifies cloaking by correlating response divergence across multiple request profiles to the same URL: when a domain returns substantially different HTTP response codes, content lengths, or redirect targets for scanner versus residential visitor profiles within a detection window, it indicates intentional cloaking. Supports TP-0042 Phase 3 detection of TDS cloaking used to evade automated threat scanning and URL reputation systems.

objects.name: TDS Shared Infrastructure Correlation
objects.description: Detects domains from different apparent campaigns sharing hosting infrastructure, nameservers, or registration patterns — indicating a common TDS operator serving multiple affiliates. This rule performs graph-based correlation by identifying domains resolving to the same IP CIDR block with different registrant information but similar registration timing. TDS operators frequently reuse backend infrastructure across campaigns while rotating customer-facing domains, creating detectable infrastructure overlap patterns. Shared nameserver configurations, co-located IP assignments within the same /24 CIDR, and registration timestamps clustered within hours are strong indicators of centralized TDS management across ostensibly independent fraud campaigns.

objects.name: AI-Generated Domain Lexical Pattern Detection
objects.description: Detects domain registrations exhibiting lexical patterns consistent with AI-generated names: natural-language-like domain names that are grammatically plausible but not established brands, unusual TLD selection patterns, and registration in bulk with similar lexical characteristics. Large language models can produce domain names that bypass traditional DGA detection because they use real words and plausible constructions rather than random character strings. This rule identifies clusters of newly registered domains sharing lexical similarity scores above threshold, exhibiting natural-language n-gram distributions, and registered through the same registrar within a compressed time window. AI-generated domain portfolios tend to follow detectable stylistic patterns such as consistent word-count, hyphenation style, and semantic category clustering that distinguish them from organic registrations.

objects.name: Bulk Let's Encrypt Certificate Issuance Clustering
objects.description: Detects clusters of Let's Encrypt certificate issuances for domains sharing nameserver or registrar characteristics within a short time window. RDGA and AI-generated campaigns frequently provision certificates in bulk immediately after registration to enable HTTPS on fraudulent landing pages and phishing sites. Legitimate bulk certificate issuance typically occurs through established organizations with consistent registration history. This rule identifies anomalous spikes in certificate issuance where multiple domains share infrastructure indicators such as common nameservers, registrar, or IP allocation, and certificates are issued within hours of domain registration. The combination of rapid registration-to-certificate timing and shared infrastructure strongly indicates coordinated fraudulent domain provisioning for campaign deployment.

objects.name: Zone File Daily Diff Anomaly Detection
objects.description: Detects anomalous patterns in daily zone file diffs: unusual volume of new registrations in a single TLD, concentration of registrations at specific registrars, or patterns suggesting algorithmic generation including lexical similarity, sequential naming, and entropy clustering. Zone file diffs provide a ground-truth view of new domain registrations across gTLDs and many ccTLDs. Fraudulent campaigns using RDGA, TDS, or AI-generated domain strategies produce detectable statistical anomalies in daily diff data — particularly registrar concentration spikes, abnormal per-TLD registration volumes, and clusters of domains with similar character distribution or word structure. This rule establishes rolling baselines for registrar-TLD combinations and alerts when daily new registration counts exceed three standard deviations from the 30-day rolling mean, or when entropy analysis reveals clustering indicative of algorithmic or template-based domain generation.

objects.name: State-Criminal Shared Infrastructure Overlap
objects.description: Detect when IP addresses, nameservers, or hosting infrastructure previously attributed to state-sponsored threat actors begin hosting domains or services associated with criminal campaigns (or vice versa). Uses graph-based detection to identify shared IP CIDR blocks, nameserver overlap, and temporal proximity of domain registrations. State-criminal convergence represents an emerging threat where nation-state infrastructure is repurposed for financially motivated crime, or criminal bulletproof hosting serves dual-use purposes for both espionage and fraud operations. This detection correlates threat intelligence attribution data with passive DNS records and infrastructure registration metadata to surface shared hosting patterns across historically distinct threat actor categories.

objects.name: Sanctions Designation Infrastructure Migration
objects.description: Detect infrastructure migration patterns following OFAC sanctions designations. Domains previously resolving to sanctioned entity IP ranges migrate to new hosting within 7-30 days of designation, retaining similar DNS configurations but different IP blocks. Tracks Aeza to Smart Digital/Datavice and Garantex to Grinex migration patterns. Sanctions designations trigger predictable infrastructure migration behavior where sanctioned entities rapidly move domains and services to new IP ranges while preserving nameserver configurations, MX records, and SSL certificate patterns. This detection correlates OFAC designation dates with zone file diffs and passive DNS records to identify domains that migrate from sanctioned IP ranges to new hosting within the expected evasion window, flagging infrastructure that retains structural DNS similarity despite IP block changes.

objects.name: Stablecoin Settlement Pattern Anomaly
objects.description: Detect stablecoin transaction patterns consistent with sanctions evasion settlement. Identifies Monday-Friday volume surges with weekend drops (business settlement pattern), transaction clustering to known no-KYC exchange addresses, and volume patterns matching the A7A5 ruble-backed stablecoin profile. Sanctions evasion through stablecoin settlement produces distinctive temporal patterns that mirror traditional business settlement cycles rather than typical retail crypto trading behavior. The weekday-to-weekend volume ratio, combined with clustering of transactions to addresses associated with no-KYC exchanges, provides a high-confidence signal for institutional sanctions evasion activity. This detection establishes rolling baselines for address-level volume patterns and alerts when weekday-weekend ratios and exchange clustering metrics exceed defined thresholds.

objects.name: BPH Rebranding Chain Detection
objects.description: Detect bulletproof hosting providers that rebrand following law enforcement or sanctions action. Identifies new hosting entities advertising the same IP ranges, same BGP ASN prefixes, or same upstream transit providers as recently sanctioned or seized BPH operations. Tracks the Garantex to Grinex and Aeza to Smart Digital/Datavice patterns. Bulletproof hosting providers under sanctions or law enforcement pressure follow predictable rebranding patterns — registering new corporate entities while retaining the same underlying network infrastructure. BGP route announcements, IP range allocations, and upstream transit provider relationships persist across rebrandings, providing durable detection signals. This rule monitors for new hosting entities that share ASN prefixes, IP CIDR blocks, or transit provider relationships with recently sanctioned or seized BPH operations within a 90-day window following enforcement action.

objects.name: Election-Cycle Domain Registration Spike
objects.description: Detect anomalous increases in domain registrations containing financial institution brand names or financial services keywords during election periods. Compares registration volumes against a 90-day rolling baseline, alerting on 3x+ increases within 30 days of scheduled elections. Integrates with election calendar data for predictive detection.

objects.name: Sanctions-Announcement Infrastructure Correlation
objects.description: Detect correlations between OFAC/EU sanctions announcements and subsequent infrastructure changes. Identifies new domain registrations by sanctioned entity-linked registrars, IP block migrations, and new BGP announcements from previously quiet ASNs within 14 days of sanctions designation.

objects.name: Politically-Motivated DDoS Financial Sector Targeting
objects.description: Detect Layer 7 DNS attack patterns targeting financial services infrastructure that correlate with geopolitical event timelines. Differentiates politically motivated DDoS from criminal extortion DDoS by examining claim attribution (Telegram channel claims), target selection patterns (geopolitically aligned targets), and timing correlation with political events.

objects.name: Pig Butchering Domain Infrastructure Clustering
objects.description: Detect clusters of domains exhibiting pig butchering investment platform characteristics: similar page structures, cryptocurrency wallet integration, registration through privacy-protected registrars, hosted on known scam compound infrastructure IP ranges. Documents Funnull-pattern CNAME clustering.

objects.name: Scam Compound Cryptocurrency Payment Infrastructure
objects.description: Detect domain clusters with cryptocurrency payment page patterns (wallet address display, QR code generation, transaction verification) registered in bulk through shared registrar/nameserver infrastructure.

objects.name: BPH IP Block Migration Post-Sanctions
objects.description: Detect IP address blocks previously associated with sanctioned or seized BPH providers appearing under new BGP announcements from different ASNs. Track continuity of malicious hosting through IP block ownership changes.

objects.name: Cloud Provider IP Abuse for BPH Resale
objects.description: Detect patterns consistent with legitimate cloud provider IP blocks being resold for BPH: unusual CNAME density (100+ domains per IP), diverse domain registrants sharing the same cloud IP range, and high abuse-report-to-domain ratios. Documents Funnull-pattern indicators (332K domains across 548 CNAMEs).

objects.name: CNAME Clustering for DGA Domain Networks
objects.description: Detect anomalous CNAME record density where hundreds or thousands of apparently unrelated domains share CNAME chains terminating at a small number of infrastructure endpoints. Indicates centrally managed infrastructure reusing cloud or CDN providers for mass domain hosting.

objects.name: CMLN Wallet Cluster Velocity
objects.description: Detect cryptocurrency wallet clusters exhibiting CMLN operational characteristics: high transaction velocity (average processing time under 2 minutes), incoming transfers from multiple unrelated sources, and rapid outbound distribution to exchange or OTC wallets.

objects.name: No-KYC Exchange Off-Ramp Pattern
objects.description: Detect cryptocurrency flows matching the DPRK 45-day laundering cycle pattern: initial rapid distancing through DeFi protocols (days 1-5), integration through no-KYC exchanges (days 5-14), and off-ramping through Chinese OTC brokers (days 20-45). Temporal pattern matching against known laundering cycle timelines.

objects.name: DaaS Platform Transaction Pattern
objects.description: Detect cryptocurrency transactions matching Deepfake-as-a-Service (DaaS) subscription patterns: recurring payments of $100-$1,000/month to wallets associated with known deepfake service providers, or one-time payments of $50-$500 for per-use deepfake generation services. These patterns indicate procurement of deepfake tooling used in downstream fraud operations including identity verification bypass and social engineering.

objects.name: Real-Time Face/Voice Changer Detection During Video Interview
objects.description: Detect real-time face and voice changing artifacts during video conferencing sessions: (1) virtual camera driver interception via OBS Virtual Camera, ManyCam, or DeepFaceLive, (2) audio spectral anomalies indicating synthetic voice generation or unnatural formant transitions, (3) temporal inconsistencies between lip movement and audio exceeding 200ms delta. These techniques are used by DPRK IT workers and other threat actors to impersonate identities during remote hiring interviews and ongoing employment.

objects.name: Multilingual Chatbot Scam Pattern Detection
objects.description: Detect messaging patterns consistent with AI chatbot-initiated scam contact: (1) unusually consistent response timing with less than 2 second variance indicating automated replies, (2) scripted conversation progression matching known romance scam, investment scam, or pig-butchering templates, (3) language switching mid-conversation to target victims in their native language, (4) identical or near-identical phrasing across multiple reported conversation instances. These patterns are characteristic of scam compound operations using multilingual AI chatbots to scale social engineering.

objects.name: Automated Mule Account Creation Velocity
objects.description: Detect automated account opening patterns indicative of mule account infrastructure buildout: (1) multiple applications originating from the same device fingerprint or IP address within a 24-hour window, (2) KYC document metadata anomalies such as identical creation timestamps or template-based formatting, (3) application completion in under 2 minutes suggesting automation, (4) absence of mouse movement or scroll events with rapid sequential field completion indicating bot-driven form filling.

objects.name: KYC Verification Bot Circumvention Detection
objects.description: Detect automated circumvention of KYC identity verification processes: (1) liveness check submissions exhibiting synthetic face indicators such as GAN artifacts or uniform skin texture, (2) document photo lighting conditions inconsistent with selfie environment suggesting pre-captured or generated images, (3) multiple verification attempts from geographically dispersed IP addresses using the same identity documents, (4) session duration and interaction patterns matching known automation tooling.

objects.name: Investment TDS Geo-Routing to Legitimate Platform
objects.description: Detect Traffic Distribution System (TDS) geo-routing patterns used in investment scam infrastructure: (1) same domain resolving to different IP addresses based on requester geography, (2) US-based visitors redirected to legitimate financial services such as eToro or Coinbase while non-US visitors are routed to newly registered scam domains, (3) CNAME records functioning as TDS routing mechanisms as observed in Savvy Seahorse campaigns. This evasion technique allows scam operators to avoid detection by security researchers and law enforcement in specific jurisdictions.

objects.name: DPRK Internal Platform Network Connection Detection
objects.description: Detect connections to DPRK-associated internal collaboration platforms OConnect VPN and NetKey VPN, identified by Flare and IBM X-Force as tools used by DPRK IT workers: (1) VPN connections to known OConnect or NetKey IP address ranges, (2) DNS queries resolving OConnect or NetKey domains, (3) VPN protocol signatures matching OConnect or NetKey handshake patterns, particularly from endpoints that are simultaneously connected to corporate VPN infrastructure. Dual-VPN usage is a strong indicator of DPRK IT worker activity on compromised enterprise networks.

objects.name: Keitaro/Binom TDS Abuse Infrastructure Detection
objects.description: Detect abuse of legitimate Traffic Distribution Systems Keitaro and Binom for fraud infrastructure: (1) HTTP redirect chains containing Keitaro tracking parameters such as click_id, campaign_id, and characteristic Keitaro URL path structures, (2) domains resolving to IP addresses associated with Keitaro or Binom hosting infrastructure, (3) redirect chain behavior patterns matching cloaking and visitor fingerprinting techniques used to evade security researchers while directing victims to investment scam landing pages.

objects.name: TAE Infrastructure Rotation Detection
objects.description: Detect Threat Actor Ecosystem (TAE) infrastructure rotation patterns used by bulletproof hosting providers to evade sanctions and takedowns: (1) IP prefix transfers between related Autonomous Systems within short timeframes, (2) RIPE NCC resource reallocation to newly created organizations with minimal operational history, (3) BGP announcement changes matching known TAE rebranding patterns such as Aeza to Hypercore to NetCrafters, (4) threat density score spikes on newly announced prefixes indicating migration of malicious infrastructure to fresh address space.

objects.name: UCP Cart Mandate Gift Card Injection via Indirect Prompt Injection
objects.description: Detects unauthorized gift card line items appended to UCP Cart Mandate payloads by AI shopping agents whose context has been compromised via indirect prompt injection. Threat actors create deals aggregator or coupon sites containing hidden payloads that reprogram the agent's memory during browsing. The agent then appends a hidden digital gift card line item to the Cart Mandate JSON-RPC payload with the recipient email set to an attacker-controlled address and display_status set to hidden. The additional cost may be disguised as Tax/Fees in the user's UI. This rule targets Phase 3-4 (Positioning/Execution) of the attack, detecting the presence of gift card items with suspicious recipient addresses or hidden display status in checkout payloads.

objects.name: UCP Returns Logic Hijacking — Void Return and Verify Step Bypass
objects.description: Detects exploitation of the UCP returns state machine where AI agents skip the order.return.verify step and trigger settlement.refund.instant() using fraudulent tracking IDs (e.g., void-000). Threat actors embed hidden instructions in product page HTML metadata or invisible span tags that are ingested by the agent when it reads return instructions. The agent then processes the malicious command as a high-priority system update, bypassing return verification and issuing refunds without valid shipping confirmation. At scale, organized crime groups deploy bot farms to initiate thousands of void returns per hour, potentially liquidating a retailer's cash reserves. This rule targets Phase 4 (Execution) by detecting refund primitives triggered without proper verification, void tracking IDs, and anomalous refund velocity.

objects.name: Indirect Prompt Injection in UCP Agent Browsing Content
objects.description: Detects indicators of indirect prompt injection payloads in web content encountered by UCP shopping agents during autonomous browsing. Because UCP agents are designed to autonomously browse, summarize and interact with merchant sites, they are highly susceptible to indirect prompt injection where the attack is not typed by the user but encountered by the agent while performing a task. Threat actors embed hidden payloads in deals aggregator sites, coupon pages, product listings, and merchant pages using techniques including invisible text, hidden HTML span tags, metadata-embedded instructions, and CSS-hidden content. These payloads target the agent's context window to reprogram behavior — appending hidden Cart Mandate line items, bypassing return verification steps, or redirecting transactions. This rule targets Phase 2 (Initial Access) by scanning agent-ingested content for prompt injection indicators before they can compromise agent behavior.

objects.name: TDS URL Parameter Fingerprint Tracking Across Rotating Domains
objects.description: Detects consistent URL query parameter patterns (TDS software behavioral signatures) appearing across multiple rotating domains, indicating a single TDS operator managing infrastructure through domain rotation. TDS operators require consistent parameter schemas to route traffic between affiliates, track conversions, and attribute payouts — these parameters are the TDS internal API contract visible in redirect URLs even when domain names rotate. The VexTrio TDS was tracked for years via its distinctive ?u=&o= query parameter format before corporate attribution was achieved (Black Hat USA 2025, Infoblox). This rule identifies recurring parameter fingerprints across newly registered or rapidly rotating domains as indicators of TDS infrastructure managed by a single operator.

objects.name: Blank Credit Card Subscription Fraud Pattern Detection
objects.description: Detects patterns consistent with blank credit card subscription fraud as operated by VexTrio/Ad Trafficko and similar affiliate fraud platforms. In this scheme, affiliates deploy customizable credit card capture templates offering low-cost items ("Free iPhone, $1.99 shipping" or "Walmart gift card, $0.99 shipping"). Victims enter card details believing they are paying a nominal fee; the platform charges a higher amount ($9.99 typical) and enrolls them in recurring subscriptions generating ongoing charges. Affiliate payouts reach $120 per successful lead. This rule targets the transaction monitoring layer to identify: (1) initial nominal-amount card-not-present charges from newly registered or unknown merchants followed by recurring charges at higher amounts, (2) merchant descriptor patterns consistent with subscription enrollment services, (3) high chargeback ratios from merchants exhibiting these patterns. Source: Black Hat USA 2025 (Infoblox VexTrio deanonymization).

objects.name: Fake Mobile App Residential Proxy and Subscription Scam Detection
objects.description: Detects indicators of fake mobile applications that function as residential proxies or subscription scams, as documented in the VexTrio fake app operations (Black Hat USA 2025, Infoblox). VexTrio operated fake mobile apps for 7-8 years through Google Play Store, Apple App Store, and third-party forums. Three categories: (1) Fake VPNs that route user traffic through residential proxy networks (making users unwitting proxy nodes) with keyword-scanning capabilities targeting banking and personal information, (2) Fake Android cleaners (device optimization tools), (3) Fake spam/notification protection apps that operate a self-referential scam cycle — after push notification abuse infects the victim browser (100-150 notifications/day), victim is served an ad for a "spam protection" app that requests permissions to disable browser notifications, displays fabricated "blocked" notification screens, then transitions to $6.99/week subscription after 24 hours. This rule detects network-level and endpoint-level indicators of these app categories.

objects.name: Rapid Enrollment-to-Billing Healthcare Provider Anomaly
objects.description: Detects healthcare providers (DME suppliers, hospice agencies, home health companies, ABA therapy providers) that begin submitting claims at high volume within 30 days of Medicare/Medicaid enrollment. Operation Gold Rush (DOJ 2025) documented a Russian-Estonian TCO that acquired 30+ legitimate DME companies and immediately submitted $10.6 billion in fraudulent claims using stolen identities. The rapid enrollment-to-billing pattern is the highest-confidence indicator of fraudulent provider intent: legitimate providers typically require months to establish patient relationships, credentialing, and operational infrastructure before reaching significant billing volume. This rule flags providers billing >$100,000 within 30 days of enrollment, with additional risk scoring for providers concentrated in known high-fraud geographic areas and providers with high single-code billing ratios.

objects.name: Single-Code Billing Concentration and Impossible Day Healthcare Fraud
objects.description: Detects two high-confidence healthcare billing fraud indicators: (1) Single-code billing concentration — providers billing overwhelmingly one HCPCS/CPT code, where a single code exceeds 80% of total claims. Operation Gold Rush documented a TCO that submitted $10.6 billion in fraudulent claims concentrated on urinary catheters and continuous glucose monitors. Legitimate providers bill across diverse code sets reflecting varied patient needs. (2) Impossible day billing — providers billing more than 24 hours of procedures in a single calendar day, a mathematical impossibility indicating phantom billing or systematic upcoding. Both patterns are documented in DOJ 2025 National Healthcare Fraud Takedown prosecutions and CrimsonVector Security threat analysis. Source: CrimsonVector Security March 2026; DOJ Operation Gold Rush June 2025.

objects.name: Ghost Patient Claims and Geographic Provider Clustering Detection
objects.description: Detects two healthcare fraud patterns: (1) Ghost patient claims — Medicare/Medicaid claims submitted for deceased, incarcerated, or relocated beneficiaries who could not have received the billed services. Operation Gold Rush exploited over 1 million stolen American identities including elderly and disabled individuals. (2) Geographic provider clustering — ZIP codes with anomalous concentrations of healthcare providers and high average billing per provider, indicating shell company clustering. LA County has 1,923 registered hospice providers (more than 36 states combined), with 7 of 14 entities in one LA plaza having zero CMS data. GAO reports found approximately 22% of practice locations in PECOS were potentially ineligible including UPS Store mailboxes and vacant addresses. Source: CrimsonVector Security March 2026; DOJ 2025 National Healthcare Fraud Takedown; GAO-15-448.

objects.name: Recovery Fraud Contact Pattern — Payments from Recent Fraud Victims to Unfamiliar Recipients
objects.description: Detects potential recovery fraud by identifying payments from customers who filed fraud complaints within the preceding 90 days to previously unseen recipient accounts. Recovery fraud operators re-contact prior fraud victims posing as recovery agents, lawyers, or government officials, extracting additional fees for purported fund recovery. This rule correlates complaint records with subsequent outbound payment activity to flag secondary victimization.

objects.name: Mass-Marketing Fraud Burst Calling Pattern — SIM Farm and Robodialling Detection
objects.description: Detects burst patterns from potential SIM farm or robodialling infrastructure targeting customer phone numbers. Mass-marketing fraud infrastructure uses sequential phone numbers, short call durations (most calls rejected), and high-volume outbound calling to reach victims at scale. This rule identifies inbound calling patterns characteristic of organized boiler room operations, including sequential source number prefixes, short call duration clustering, and geographic origin mismatch between caller ID display and actual call routing.

objects.name: Long-Firm Credit Buildup Pattern — Steady Low Utilization Followed by Rapid Spike
objects.description: Detects commercial accounts following a long-firm fraud pattern: steady low-value credit utilization for 6-12 months (building creditworthiness) followed by rapid escalation in credit utilization (the "burst"). Long-firm fraud involves organized criminal groups establishing businesses, building credit relationships, then exploiting that trust to defraud supply chain partners and trade finance banks. The artificially smooth buildup period followed by a discontinuous spike is the hallmark behavioral indicator.

objects.name: Staged Accident Claim Correlation — Shared Professional Enabler Network Detection
objects.description: Detects potential organized crash-for-cash insurance fraud rings by identifying claims from multiple ostensibly unrelated accidents that share common professional enablers (same medical provider, legal representative, or repair shop). Organized insurance fraud rings rely on networks of corrupt professionals who process claims across multiple staged incidents. The shared professional enabler network is the most durable and detectable element of the ring, as replacing trusted corrupt professionals is harder than recruiting new participants.

objects.name: AiTM Session Token Replay Detection — User-Agent and IP Mismatch Post-MFA
objects.description: Detects potential Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) session token replay by identifying User-Agent string or IP address mismatches between MFA completion events and subsequent session access events. AiTM phishing kits capture session tokens during MFA relay, then replay them from attacker infrastructure with different User-Agent/IP characteristics. Sekoia.io identified 11 major AiTM kits (Tycoon 2FA most prevalent: 1,200+ domains, 500K+ organizations/month). FIDO2 blocks 93.9% of AiTM campaigns.

objects.name: Post-Compromise Inbox Rule Manipulation — Rule Creation After New-IP Authentication
objects.description: Detects inbox rule creation or modification within 24 hours of a sign-in from a previously unseen IP address. AiTM phishing kit operators create inbox rules within minutes of session hijack to redirect payment notifications, delete security alerts, and intercept colleague communications. Rules forwarding to external domains or deleting emails matching specific sender/subject patterns are high-confidence indicators of post-compromise activity.

objects.name: AI-Generated Phishing Content Stylometric Detection
objects.description: Detects AI-generated phishing content using stylometric features. Research shows XGBoost with 60 stylometric features detects GPT-4o-generated phishing with 96% accuracy and 99% AUC. Key features: imperative verb count, clause density, first-person pronoun usage, urgency markers, authority indicators, sentiment manipulation, financial trigger words, and semantic inconsistency. DetectGPT achieves ~0.95 AUROC via zero-shot statistical signatures.
