This rule defines the feature extraction pipeline and scoring thresholds for deployment in email security and fraud communication analysis systems.

objects.name: Cialdini Persuasion Principle Scoring in Fraud Communications
objects.description: Scores inbound communications (email, SMS, chat) for Cialdini's six principles of persuasion: Reciprocity, Consistency, Social Proof, Authority, Liking, and Scarcity. Research shows combining these features with BERT/SBERT embeddings improves phishing detection F1 by 2.62%. Communications exhibiting 3+ principles above threshold are flagged as high-probability social engineering. Directly applicable to romance fraud, investment scam, impersonation, and recovery fraud detection where psychological manipulation is the primary attack vector.

objects.name: SIM Swap Network-Level API Detection — Pre-MFA SIM Change Verification
objects.description: Detects potential SIM swap attacks by querying network-level APIs before MFA code delivery. SIM swap fraud surged 1,055% in the UK (3,000 cases in 2024). Three network-level APIs provide the most effective detection: SIM Swap Check (has the SIM been changed recently?), Number Verification (is the number still assigned to the expected device?), and Call Forwarding Signal (is call forwarding active?). Correlating positive signals from these APIs with subsequent MFA authentication attempts provides high-confidence SIM swap detection.

objects.name: Crypto Token Rug Pull Early Warning — On-Chain and OSINT Indicators
objects.description: Detects cryptocurrency rug pull / exit scam indicators using on-chain and OSINT signals. Rug pulls constituted 68% of all crypto scams in 2025 (350+ cases 2024). On-chain indicators: Uniswap liquidity removal >80% in single transaction, token holder concentration (top 5 holders >60%), contract functions with hidden mint/pause/ blacklist capabilities. OSINT indicators: social media silence after promotion burst, developer wallet activity cessation, Telegram/Discord channel deletion. Critical finding: OSINT signals precede on-chain anomalies by days or weeks.

objects.name: Employment Fraud Metadata Feature Detection
objects.description: Detects fraudulent job postings using metadata features from the EMSCAD benchmark (18,000 samples). Key finding: when both telecommuting and company logo flags equal zero, there is a 92% probability of fraud. Geographic concentration patterns (e.g., Bakersfield 15:1 fake-to-real ratio) provide additional signal. DistilBERT+SMOTE models achieve strong results; DNNs reach ~98% accuracy. This rule implements the high-confidence metadata feature checks that require no NLP processing.

objects.name: Gift Card Balance Probing Velocity Detection
objects.description: Detects automated gift card balance probing by monitoring balance check endpoints for high-velocity requests. NRF RFT FT1103 documents that fraudsters abuse legitimate balance check functions (web app, phone IVR) to identify funded cards from brute-forced or purchased card number lists. Detection signals include request velocity per IP/device, VoIP source numbers, off-hours timing, and device fingerprint anomalies. Gift card balance probing is a precursor to gift card redemption fraud, card merging, and resale monetization.

objects.name: Gift Card Merge and Transfer Anomaly Detection
objects.description: Detects suspicious gift card merge and transfer activity indicating value consolidation from multiple illicit sources. NRF RFT FT1202 documents that fraudsters transfer value from multiple illicitly obtained gift cards to a single legitimate card — e.g., 20 cards with $5 merged into one $255 card. This consolidation is a key Control phase technique enabling subsequent monetization. Detection signals include merge velocity, source card count, and correlation with recent suspicious balance check activity.

objects.name: AiTM Session Token Replay — Same SessionId from Multiple IPs
objects.description: Detects potential AiTM session token replay by identifying the same Entra ID SessionId appearing from multiple IP addresses within a short time window. In an AiTM attack, the phishing proxy IP and the attacker's actual replay IP both appear on the same session. This is the single strongest AiTM detection signal in Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs. Additional confidence comes from the error code sequence 50074 (MFA required) → 50140 (Keep Me Signed In) → 0 (success) in rapid succession with medium or high risk level.

objects.name: Sneaky 2FA Impossible Device Shift — User-Agent Mismatch per Auth Step
objects.description: Detects the "impossible device shift" signature characteristic of Sneaky 2FA and related AiTM phishing kits. Sneaky 2FA uses different hardcoded User-Agent strings per authentication step — Safari on iOS for the Login:login step and Edge on Windows for the Login:resume step. This pattern is detectable via correlation of mismatched User-Agents within the same correlation ID within 10 minutes. This detection also catches Dadsec (missing User-Agent), Tycoon 2FA (rare User-Agent values), and W3LL OV6 (inconsistent UAs).

objects.name: Rockstar 2FA / FlowerStorm Application ID and User-Agent Detection
objects.description: Detects sign-ins associated with the Rockstar 2FA and FlowerStorm AiTM phishing kits (Storm-1575 lineage) by matching the hardcoded Office365 Application ID and User-Agent string used by these kits. Rockstar 2FA and its successor FlowerStorm use the Office365 Application ID 72782ba9-4490-4f03-8d82-562370ea3566 combined with the hardcoded User-Agent string containing "WebView/3.0" — a high-fidelity detection signature with very low false positive rate. FlowerStorm surged within ~10 days of Rockstar 2FA's infrastructure collapse in November 2024.

objects.name: Smishing Triad Domain Pattern and iMessage/RCS Delivery Detection
objects.description: Detects indicators of Smishing Triad phishing infrastructure including Darcula/Magic Cat domain patterns and Chenlun kit fingerprints. The Smishing Triad ecosystem has generated 194,000+ malicious domains targeting users in 121+ countries, compromising 884,000+ credit cards. Darcula domains follow a "com-" prefix pattern. Chenlun kits are fingerprinted by the presence of ResourceRedConfig.js and /ResourceConfig/urlConfig.json files. Detection also covers toll-scam lure patterns (E-ZPass, SunPass, FasTrak, I-Pass) commonly used in smishing campaigns.

objects.name: Post-AiTM Inbox Rule Manipulation — New Rules from Risky Sign-In
objects.description: Detects inbox rule creation or modification in Exchange Online following a sign-in flagged with medium or high risk, or following authentication from a previously unseen IP address. Post-AiTM inbox rule manipulation is a characteristic Phase 3 (Positioning) technique: within minutes of session hijack, attackers create inbox rules to redirect or delete security alerts, payment notifications, and colleague communications. This detection correlates Exchange Online Unified Audit Log operations (New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule, Set-Mailbox forwarding) with Entra ID risky sign-in events.

objects.name: Synthetic Identity Credit Utilization Spike — Low-and-Slow Buildup Followed by Bust-Out
objects.description: Detects the characteristic synthetic identity bust-out pattern: prolonged low credit utilization (< 35% for 6+ months) followed by a rapid spike to near-maximum utilization (> 80%) within 30 days. Synthetic identity fraudsters nurture credit profiles over 12-24 months with steady payments and low utilization, then execute a coordinated bust-out where all available credit is maxed simultaneously. The Federal Reserve estimates synthetic identity fraud costs U.S. lenders $6B+ annually. The discontinuous utilization jump from a stable baseline is the hallmark behavioral indicator.

objects.name: Thin-File Identity Clustering — Shared Address, Phone, or Device Across New Applicants
objects.description: Detects clusters of thin-file credit applicants sharing physical addresses, phone numbers, or device fingerprints — a hallmark indicator of synthetic identity ring activity. Fraud rings fabricate multiple synthetic identities that share infrastructure (mailing addresses, burner phones, devices used for applications). When 3+ new applicants with thin credit files (< 12 months history, < 3 tradelines) share an address, phone, or device within a 180-day window, this indicates coordinated identity fabrication rather than coincidental overlap. The Federal Reserve identifies address and device clustering as primary synthetic identity detection signals.

objects.name: Coordinated Bust-Out Timing — Simultaneous Max-Utilization Across Multiple Products
objects.description: Detects coordinated bust-out execution where the same identity (or linked identities) max out credit across multiple products within a 72-hour window. Synthetic identity rings time their bust-out to extract maximum value before accounts are frozen: cash advances, balance transfers to controlled accounts, and high-value purchases for resale all occur within a narrow window. When 3+ credit products associated with the same identity show utilization above 90% within 72 hours, and at least one involves a cash advance or balance transfer, this is a high-confidence bust-out indicator.

objects.name: SSN Age and Issuance Mismatch — Synthetic Identity Indicator
objects.description: Detects credit applications where the SSN characteristics are inconsistent with the applicant's stated identity — a primary indicator of synthetic identity fabrication. Key signals: (1) SSN issued after the applicant's date of birth suggests the SSN belongs to someone else (minors, immigrants, recently deceased), (2) post-2011 randomized SSNs that don't match SSA area number geography, (3) SSN first appearing at credit bureaus within the last 18 months combined with an applicant age > 25 (natural credit profiles start appearing at 18-22). The eCBSV (electronic Consent Based SSN Verification) service can confirm SSN-name-DOB matches, but adoption is inconsistent.

objects.name: First-Party Credit Buildup and Sudden Spike
objects.description: Detects consumer accounts following a first-party fraud pattern: steady good payments for 6-12 months then sudden utilization spike and missed payments within 60 days. Unlike synthetic identity (TP-0003), the identity is real but the intent is fraudulent. First-party bust-out actors nurture credit profiles with consistent on-time payments and low utilization, then rapidly maximize available credit before abandoning the account. The transition from responsible usage to aggressive drawdown is the key behavioral signal. LexisNexis estimates first-party fraud now represents 36% of all detected fraud events globally.

objects.name: Never-Pay Pattern — Immediate Max Utilization with Zero Payments
objects.description: Detects new credit accounts with immediate high utilization and zero payment activity after 60 days — classic "never-pay" first-party fraud where the consumer opens an account with no intent to pay. Unlike bust-out schemes that involve a credit nurturing phase, never-pay actors maximize utilization immediately after account opening and make no payments whatsoever. This pattern is distinguishable from legitimate new account activity because at least one billing cycle has passed with zero payment response. The never-pay variant accounts for a significant share of first-party fraud losses, particularly in unsecured credit products.

objects.name: Rapid Authorized User Addition Across Multiple Accounts
objects.description: Detects the same individual being added as an authorized user across 3 or more credit accounts within 30 days. This technique is used in first-party bust-out and synthetic identity schemes to rapidly build credit history or gain access to multiple credit lines for coordinated bust-out. Authorized user tradelines inherit the primary account's payment history, allowing fraudsters to artificially inflate credit scores in weeks rather than months. When combined with subsequent high utilization, this pattern is a strong leading indicator of coordinated bust-out activity. The "piggybacking" of authorized user status is a well-documented credit manipulation technique exploited by both first-party fraudsters and synthetic identity rings.

objects.name: Document Metadata Anomaly — AI-Generated ID Document Detection
objects.description: Detects submitted identity documents with metadata inconsistencies indicating AI generation or manipulation: PDF creation tools (Photoshop, GIMP, AI generators), timestamp manipulation (creation date after modification date), inconsistent DPI, missing EXIF data, font embedding anomalies. 85% of synthetic fraud now involves GenAI document fabrication. Underground services like OnlyFake and ProKYC produce photo-realistic government IDs for as little as $30, complete with simulated holograms and barcode data, but leave detectable metadata and structural artifacts that differ from genuine document scans.

objects.name: Facial Liveness Failure Pattern — Iterative Deepfake Tuning
objects.description: Detects repeated liveness check failures from the same device followed by eventual success — indicates iterative deepfake tuning where fraudsters adjust their deepfake parameters until they pass liveness detection. Normal users fail once (bad lighting) and succeed quickly; attackers show a pattern of 3+ failures with improving scores. Real-time face-swap applications and pre-recorded deepfake videos are used to defeat challenges requiring head turns, blinking, or phrase repetition. The iterative improvement pattern — each attempt scoring higher than the last — is a strong indicator of adversarial tuning against the liveness detection model.

objects.name: Cross-Application Identity Collision — Same Biometric or Device Across Different Identities
objects.description: Detects the same biometric template (face embedding), device fingerprint, or behavioral pattern appearing across applications submitted under different identity names. Fraudsters using AI-generated faces may reuse the same base model or device, creating detectable collisions in the biometric or device space. Even when AI-generated facial images appear visually distinct, the underlying face embedding vectors may cluster due to shared generative model artifacts. Similarly, device fingerprints and behavioral biometric profiles persist across sessions even when the presented identity changes, enabling cross-application correlation that reveals synthetic identity networks.

objects.name: AI Document Template Cluster — Identical Formatting Patterns Across Applications
objects.description: Detects clusters of submitted ID documents sharing identical formatting artifacts, template structures, or AI generation signatures. AI document generators produce documents with consistent pixel-level artifacts, font embedding patterns, and template metadata even when the identity details differ. When 3+ documents from different applicants show template_similarity_score > 0.85, this indicates a common AI generator. Underground forgery services like OnlyFake successors use a limited number of document templates per jurisdiction, creating detectable clustering when multiple synthetic identities are onboarded through the same forgery pipeline. Template similarity analysis across the document corpus reveals these clusters even when individual documents pass automated verification checks.

objects.name: Check Washing — Altered Check Mobile Deposit with Duplicate or MICR Inconsistency
objects.description: Detects mobile deposits of potentially washed or altered checks by identifying two key indicators: (1) the same check number deposited at multiple financial institutions within a short window, indicating duplicate deposit fraud, and (2) check amounts inconsistent with the MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) line data, suggesting the payee and amount fields were chemically washed and rewritten while the MICR line was preserved. FinCEN data shows check fraud SARs surged 200%+ from 2021-2023, driven by USPS mail theft and the ease of mobile deposit. Washed checks deposited via mobile apps exploit the lag between deposit and check clearing under Reg CC funds availability requirements. The Recorded Future 2025 report documented a geographic shift in stolen check activity toward the Midwest and suburban/rural USPS routes.

objects.name: Disability Insurance Fraud — Fabricated Medical Documentation Provider Anomaly
objects.description: Detects patterns indicative of fabricated medical documentation supporting fraudulent disability claims by identifying two key signals: (1) a single medical provider billing across multiple claimants with identical or near-identical diagnosis codes (ICD-10), suggesting template-driven fabricated documentation rather than genuine clinical variation, and (2) claims supported by providers located outside the claimant's geographic area, indicating the claimant traveled specifically to a complicit provider or the documentation was fabricated remotely. DOJ prosecutions reveal organized disability fraud rings where complicit providers generate documentation for dozens of fictitious or exaggerated claims, with cumulative payouts in the millions. The long-tail nature of disability payments means a single fraudulent claim can generate $100,000+ in benefits before detection. Generative AI tools now enable fabrication of convincing medical documentation without provider collusion, representing an emerging escalation vector.

objects.name: Insider-Enabled Account Fraud — Employee Access Anomaly with Subsequent Account Changes
objects.description: Detects financial institution employees accessing customer accounts outside their normal behavioral pattern, combined with subsequent account modifications — a hallmark of insider- enabled fraud. The rule identifies four converging anomaly signals: (1) account access occurring outside normal business hours for the employee's role, (2) access volume significantly exceeding the employee's baseline, (3) access to accounts not assigned to the employee's portfolio or branch, and (4) account changes (address, beneficiary, contact info, transaction limits) following the anomalous access. The ACFE estimates insider fraud accounts for 5% of organizational revenue globally, with an average detection time of 18 months. Financial institution insiders are particularly dangerous because they understand internal controls and operate below detection thresholds. This rule correlates UEBA access data with account modification logs to surface the positioning phase (CFPF P3) before funds are extracted.

objects.name: Business Identity Takeover — Rapid Signer, Address, and Banking Detail Changes on Established Account
objects.description: Detects potential business identity takeover by identifying a cluster of critical account changes occurring within a short window on established commercial accounts. The rule flags accounts where authorized signer changes, business address updates, and banking detail modifications (routing/account number, wire instructions, or beneficiary changes) all occur within 14 days — a pattern strongly indicative of corporate hijacking. Threat actors impersonate legitimate businesses by filing fraudulent amendments with the Secretary of State to change registered agents or officers, then use the hijacked identity to modify banking relationships and extract funds. Established accounts (open 12+ months) are specifically targeted because they have built credit history and banking relationships that actors exploit. This pattern was heavily observed during pandemic-era PPP/EIDL fraud and continues to plague commercial lenders. Average commercial loan fraud via business identity theft ranges from $100K to $1M+.

objects.name: GenAI-Enhanced APP Fraud — Escalating Investment Payments to New Beneficiary
objects.description: Detects the characteristic authorized push payment (APP) pattern associated with GenAI- enhanced investment fraud (pig butchering). The rule identifies customers making increasing payments to a newly added beneficiary with investment-related payment references, where payment velocity accelerates over a multi-week period. This pattern reflects the classic fattening-then-slaughter cycle: victims are groomed through AI-powered financial advisor personas and deepfake celebrity endorsements, make a small initial investment, see fabricated returns on fraudulent trading dashboards, and are progressively encouraged to invest larger amounts. The FBI IC3 reported $6.57 billion in investment fraud losses in 2024 — the single largest fraud category. Chainalysis research shows AI-enabled investment scams extract 4.5x more revenue per operation ($3.2M average) compared to non-AI variants ($719K average). The rule targets the execution phase (P4) where escalating authorized payments represent the point of maximum financial exposure before funds are laundered through cryptocurrency mixing, DeFi protocols, or mule networks.

objects.name: Elder Financial Exploitation — New Payee Addition with Escalating Payment Amounts
objects.description: Detects a multi-signal elder financial exploitation pattern: account holder aged 65 or older adds a new payee not present in their historical payment network, followed by escalating payment amounts to that payee over a rolling 30-day window. FBI IC3 reported $4.885B in elder fraud losses in 2024 (43% YoY increase), with the true figure estimated at $28.3B when accounting for underreporting. The convergence of advanced age, new payee addition, and escalating amounts is a hallmark of romance scams, tech support fraud, government impersonation, and caregiver exploitation — all of which follow a pattern of trust-building followed by increasing financial extraction. This rule targets Phase 4 (Execution) but the escalating pattern often indicates prolonged Phase 2/3 social engineering that has already been underway for weeks or months.

objects.name: Web3 Wallet Drainer — Malicious Token Approval to Drainer Contract
objects.description: Detects wallet drainer approval phishing by identifying three high-confidence on-chain indicators: (1) token approval (approve() or increaseAllowance()) granting unlimited allowance to a contract address on known drainer threat feeds, (2) unlimited ERC-20 approvals to contracts deployed within the last 48 hours with no verified source code, or (3) rapid multi-token approvals (3+ distinct token contracts) from a single wallet to the same spender address within a 10-minute window — characteristic of automated DaaS kit multi-token harvesting. ScamSniffer reported $494M stolen via wallet drainers in 2024, with Inferno Drainer commanding 40-45% DaaS market share. The Permit/Permit2 gasless signature variant bypasses traditional on-chain approval monitoring; this rule covers the on-chain approve() path and Permit2 batch transfer events. Stolen assets are typically consolidated and bridged cross-chain within hours.

objects.name: Ghost Student Financial Aid Fraud — Multi-Signal Botnet Enrollment Detection
objects.description: Detects ghost student financial aid fraud by correlating three botnet-driven enrollment indicators: (1) multiple FAFSA applications originating from the same device fingerprint or IP address within an enrollment cycle, (2) shared bank accounts across distinct financial aid applicants (multiple student IDs disbursing to the same routing/account number), or (3) financial aid disbursements from multiple student IDs flowing to the same beneficiary account or being withdrawn at the same ATM cluster. California community colleges flagged 31-34% of applications as potentially fraudulent, and Equifax reported preventing $180M in ghost student fraud in a single year. Ghost student botnets exploit open-enrollment admissions to submit hundreds of synthetic identity applications per cycle, file FAFSA for maximum Pell Grant eligibility ($7,395/year), and extract disbursements before census date attendance verification can trigger aid return requirements.

objects.name: Calendar Invite Injection Phishing — Mass External Calendar Event Creation from New Domains
objects.description: Detects calendar injection phishing by identifying mass calendar invite creation from external sources targeting internal users, where the event body contains URLs and the organizer domain is recently registered (under 30 days) or on a high-abuse TLD. Attackers send emails containing .ics calendar attachments or Google Calendar invite links that auto-populate on victim calendars, bypassing email gateway filtering that focuses on message body and attachment analysis. An observed March 2026 campaign delivered 6,000+ emails across 10 sender domains (9 RDGA-generated on .cyou/.sbs/.click TLDs) with antivirus renewal and meeting invite lures. Calendar events persist after email deletion and re-surface via reminder notifications, creating a delayed-action social engineering vector. Recently created organizer accounts (under 7 days) sending calendar invites to 5+ internal recipients are additionally flagged as high-confidence indicators.

objects.name: QR Code Payment Fraud (Quishing) — Malicious QR Destination to Credential Harvesting Infrastructure
objects.description: Detects quishing attacks by identifying emails or messages containing QR code images where the encoded URL resolves to a recently registered domain (under 30 days), a known URL shortener redirecting to a credential harvesting page, or a domain impersonating postal services or banking institutions. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents a European modus operandi where fraudsters send fake QR codes claiming payment is available at a post office, routing victims through a fake postal site to a cloned bank login page. In a documented case, USD 110,000 was stolen through this method. The attack exploits a fundamental QR code UX gap: unlike hyperlinks, QR codes do not display a destination URL before the victim commits to following them. The subsequent 2FA device enrollment step converts credential capture into persistent account takeover, making real-time detection at the email/content analysis layer critical before the victim scans.

objects.name: Sextortion-Investment Hybrid Fraud — Small Payment Escalation to Crypto Addresses with Communication Pattern Shift
objects.description: Detects the sextortion-investment hybrid fraud pattern where a victim makes initial small payments followed by escalating amounts to cryptocurrency addresses, with the communication pattern showing a transition from social/romantic interaction to financial urgency. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents this as a globally escalating pattern where scam centre operators systematically pivot from romance/investment scripts to sextortion as a scripted operational fallback. The hallmark behavioral signature is a first-ever crypto transaction within 30 days of a new social media contact, followed by rapid escalation in both payment frequency and amount, often accompanied by messaging patterns shifting from casual/romantic to urgent/threatening language. The hybrid structure maximizes total extraction while suppressing victim reporting through shame and blackmail leverage.

objects.name: Vehicle Export Financing Fraud — Auto Loan Followed by Rapid Title Transfer or Export with Active Lien
objects.description: Detects the vehicle export financing fraud pattern where an auto loan application is approved and the financed vehicle undergoes rapid title transfer or appears in export documentation while the loan remains active and the lien is outstanding. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents this as a growing transnational fraud scheme first detected in North America in early 2024, where criminal networks use identity theft and straw buyers to obtain auto loans for high-value vehicles, then export them overseas before lenders detect fraud. The critical detection window is the period between vehicle delivery and export — often as short as 7-21 days. Key indicators include high-value vehicles (>$30,000) with high LTV ratios, fewer than 3 loan payments made, title transfer events within 60 days of origination, and GPS telematics showing vehicle departure from the borrower's stated area toward port cities or border crossings. The structural delay between loan default and fraud detection is the primary vulnerability exploited by these networks.

objects.name: Crypto Fraud-Terrorism/Narco Financing Nexus — Sanctions-Exposed Wallets and Peel Chain Patterns Through Mixing Services
objects.description: Detects the crypto-terror/narco financing nexus pattern where transactions flow to wallets with known OFAC/sanctions exposure, or exhibit peel chain patterns through cryptocurrency mixing services followed by consolidation to designated entity-linked addresses. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents two confirmed manifestations: (1) a USD 150 million cryptocurrency fraud scheme linked to Tren de Aragua laundering drug trafficking and extortion proceeds across Chile, Colombia, Venezuela, and the Iberian Peninsula; and (2) Operation Catalyst, which uncovered a USD 562 million crypto Ponzi scheme affecting 100,000+ victims across 17 countries with wallet-level links to terrorism financing in Central Africa. The detection logic targets three signatures: direct transactions to OFAC SDN-listed wallet addresses within 2 hops, peel chain patterns where funds are split into decreasingly small amounts through mixing services before reconsolidation, and co-mingling indicators where platform wallets receive both retail investor deposits and large round-number inflows from high-risk wallet clusters. This rule operates at critical severity given the terrorism and narcotics financing implications and associated OFAC blocking obligations.

objects.name: Organized Insurance Claims Fraud — Shared Professional Enablers and Claim Timing Clustering Around Policy Inception
objects.description: Detects organized insurance claims fraud patterns where the same claimant or provider appears across multiple claims with shared professional enablers (medical provider, legal representative, repair shop), or where claim timing is clustered around policy inception. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment identifies insurance fraud — notably car and medical insurance claims — as escalating globally, with Europe most impacted: the UK recorded a 25% spike in motor insurance fraud in early 2025, France detected nearly USD 1 billion in fraud in 2024, and German insurers flagged 10% of claims as suspicious with annual losses exceeding USD 7 billion. The detection logic targets two primary signatures: (1) network analysis identifying claimants, providers, legal representatives, or repair shops appearing across multiple claims — indicating an organized fraud ring with division of labor; and (2) temporal analysis identifying claims filed within 90 days of policy inception with high severity, which indicates opportunistic application fraud followed by immediate fraudulent claim filing. The combination of shared enablers and inception-proximate timing is a strong indicator of organized ring activity.

objects.name: Organized Counterfeit Goods and Non-Delivery Fraud Network — High Dispute Merchant Accounts with Drop Location Clustering and Below-Market Pricing
objects.description: Detects organized counterfeit goods and non-delivery fraud network activity by identifying merchant accounts exhibiting multiple fraud indicators simultaneously: high chargeback/dispute rates, shipping addresses clustered at known drop locations, product listings priced significantly below market value, and seller account age under 90 days with disproportionately high transaction volume. The UNODC Organized Fraud Issue Paper (2024) documents this as the most prevalent fraud category by volume, with organized criminal groups operating multi-site networks backed by dedicated money laundering infrastructure, recruited money mules, and counterfeit supply chains. Case studies from Romania, Germany, and the US show OCGs adopting formal business structures — suppliers, distribution centers, online retailers — to deceive payment providers and scale operations. The detection logic combines four signals: (1) dispute rate exceeding 2% of transactions indicating non-delivery or counterfeit complaints; (2) shipping address concentration at drop locations or mail receiving services; (3) product pricing 30%+ below market benchmarks; and (4) new seller accounts (<90 days) with anomalously high listing and transaction volume. Any two of these four indicators in combination warrant investigation.

objects.name: Magecart WebSocket Card Data Exfiltration — Payment Page to Recently Registered Domain
objects.description: Detects Magecart-style card data exfiltration via WebSocket connections from e-commerce checkout or payment pages to recently registered domains (< 90 days) that masquerade as legitimate services (analytics, CDN, jQuery). The ANY.RUN "Banks Magecart Campaign" (March 2026) documented a 24+ month campaign across 100+ domains targeting the Redsys payment system (Spain), PayPlug SAS, and generic Visa/Mastercard flows. The attack uses a multi-stage injection model: (1) obfuscated loader injected into site scripts, (2) rotating domains deliver secondary payloads, (3) DOM monitoring conceals legitimate payment buttons and injects fake payment interfaces, (4) WebSocket connections (wss://<c2>/?token=<base64>) exfiltrate full card data (BIN, PAN, expiry, CVV). WebSocket is chosen specifically to reduce visibility in traditional HTTP-based security monitoring. Detection combines three signals: WebSocket connection from a payment/checkout page context, destination domain registered within 90 days, and domain name pattern masquerading as a legitimate service (analytics, CDN, jQuery, caching). The confirmed IOC domain list from the campaign uses registrar NICENIC INTERNATIONAL GROUP, identified by Silent Push as a bulletproof registrar.

objects.name: Bulletproof Hosting ASN Connection Correlation — Traffic to Known BPH Networks
objects.description: Detects DNS resolution or network connections to IP addresses within known bulletproof hosting (BPH) Autonomous System Number (ASN) ranges, domains registered via the NiceNIC registrar, or domains using Dynamic DNS providers such as afraid.org. Silent Push (2025) documented 200+ BPH providers controlling approximately 1 million IP addresses globally. This rule correlates network traffic against a curated list of BPH ASNs identified through abuse pattern analysis, including providers with high DGA domain density, disposable abuse contact emails, shell company registrations in permissive jurisdictions, and self-declared bulletproof hosting marketing. Additionally, the rule flags domains registered through NiceNIC — a registrar favored by threat actors (including Scattered Spider and The Com) due to its requirement for a Power of Attorney to process takedown requests — and domains leveraging Dynamic DNS services that create BPH-like abuse-resistant infrastructure. Any match warrants investigation for potential fraud-enabling infrastructure, C2 communication, or criminal hosting activity.

objects.name: Cloud Phone Behavioral Anomaly — Device-Environment Decorrelation Detection
objects.description: Detects cloud phone behavioral anomalies indicative of industrial-scale dropper/mule account creation. Cloud phones — remote-access Android devices running genuine firmware on ARM hardware in data centers — pass hardware attestation and present authentic device signals, making them invisible to traditional emulator detection. This rule uses a composite scoring approach combining device-environment decorrelation signals: perpetual full battery, absence of accelerometer motion during active sessions, presence of VPN/proxy and vendor management apps, unusually high banking app density, and recent device first-seen dates. Group-IB reports cloud phone rental from $0.10/hour with pre-verified dropper accounts selling for $50–200 on darknet markets. UK APP fraud losses reached £485.2M in 2023 with dropper accounts as the top contributing factor.

objects.name: Fake OTA Domain Pattern Detection — Domains Mimicking Booking.com/Expedia/Airbnb Registered < 30 Days
objects.description: Detects web traffic to recently registered domains (< 30 days old) that mimic major Online Travel Agency brands (Booking.com, Expedia, Airbnb) using typosquatting, homoglyph substitution, or brand-adjacent naming patterns. These fake OTA domains are the primary infrastructure for travel booking fraud credential harvesting operations. NordVPN/Saily identified 4,344 active fake travel domains in 2026. Average domain lifespan is 18 days before takedown, making registration age the highest-signal detection feature. Domains serving payment form pages are critical-severity indicators.

objects.name: B4U Booking Velocity Anomaly — Same Payment Method Booking Across Multiple OTAs/Hotels in Rapid Succession
objects.description: Detects Buy-for-You (B4U) booking fraud patterns where the same payment method is used to make travel bookings across multiple OTAs, airlines, or hotel chains within a 24-hour period, especially when bookings are made for different travelers. B4U operators use stolen payment credentials to purchase travel at legitimate platforms, then resell bookings at 30-60% of face value. Sumsub estimates B4U services generate $37B in annual travel fraud losses. The velocity of bookings across disparate merchants with mismatched traveler names is the hallmark detection signal.

objects.name: IRSF Traffic Spike Detection — Abnormal Call Volume to Premium-Rate International Numbers
objects.description: Detects abnormal spikes in outbound call volume to premium-rate international number ranges, the hallmark indicator of International Revenue Share Fraud (IRSF). IRSF is the single largest telecom fraud category at $10.76B in annual losses (CFCA/TNS 2026). Fraudsters generate artificial traffic to premium-rate numbers where they hold revenue- sharing agreements, typically using compromised PBX systems or automated dialers. The detection uses z-score analysis against per-source baseline call volumes to premium-rate destinations, flagging when hourly volume exceeds 3 standard deviations. A compromised PBX can generate $50K-$500K in fraudulent charges within hours, making real-time detection critical.

objects.name: Wangiri Callback Velocity — High Volume of Short-Duration Outbound International Calls From Single Source
objects.description: Detects Wangiri ("one-ring") fraud patterns where a high volume of short-duration (< 5 seconds) outbound international calls originate from a single source, indicating subscriber callbacks to premium-rate numbers. In a Wangiri scheme, fraudsters place brief inbound calls from premium-rate numbers to trigger victim callbacks. The callbacks connect to IVR systems or premium content lines that accumulate per-minute charges. This rule detects the callback side of the attack: clusters of brief outbound international calls from individual subscribers or PBX systems to premium-rate destinations. Average victim loss is $15-$50 per callback; aggregate campaign revenues reach $100K-$1M (Subex/Akamai).

objects.name: Telecom Subscription Velocity — Multiple New Service Activations From Same Identity/Device Within 30 Days
objects.description: Detects subscription fraud patterns where the same identity or device IMEI is used to activate multiple new telecom service accounts within a 30-day window. Subscription fraud is the top concern for 53% of telecom executives (TransUnion 2025). Fraudsters use synthetic identities (TP-0003) with GenAI-generated KYC documents to open accounts across multiple carriers, acquiring subsidized flagship devices on installment plans with no payment intent. The multi-carrier activation pattern is the strongest detection signal, as legitimate customers rarely activate 3+ accounts across 2+ carriers in a 30-day period. Devices acquired through subscription fraud are resold at 60-80% of retail value on secondary markets.

objects.name: Premium SMS Billing Anomaly — Unauthorized Premium SMS Subscriptions Appearing on Accounts
objects.description: Detects unauthorized premium SMS subscriptions (cramming) appearing on customer accounts without corresponding opt-in or consent records. Premium SMS cramming generates an estimated $1.5B in unauthorized consumer charges annually (CFCA/TNS 2026). Fraudsters add premium SMS shortcode subscriptions to accounts through compromised billing APIs, social engineering of carrier support staff, or malware-initiated WAP billing triggers. The key detection signal is premium SMS subscription records that lack a corresponding customer opt-in event. Multiple premium subscriptions appearing on the same account within a 30-day window without opt-in are high-confidence cramming indicators.

objects.name: Seller Impersonation Pattern — Property Sale Initiated by Non-Resident Owner of Vacant/Unencumbered Property With Recent Contact Info Changes
objects.description: Detects the characteristic seller impersonation pattern in real estate title fraud: a property sale or title transfer is initiated on a vacant, unencumbered property where the owner is non-resident (mailing address differs from property address) and the owner's contact information has been recently changed. FBI data shows $16.6B in total real estate fraud losses (2024), with seller impersonation of vacant property owners as the fastest-growing subcategory. Fraudsters target vacant, mortgage-free properties because there is no occupant to notice and no lender monitoring the title. A risk score is computed from multiple indicators: non-resident owner, vacant property, unencumbered, recent contact changes, and below-market listing price.

objects.name: Fraudulent Deed Transfer Anomaly — Deed Recording With Document Metadata Anomalies (AI Generation Indicators) on Properties With No Prior Activity
objects.description: Detects deed recordings that exhibit document metadata anomalies indicative of AI- generated or forged documents, particularly on properties with no recent prior recording activity. The detection combines document forensic signals (AI tool signatures in PDF metadata, rapid creation timestamps, font inconsistencies) with property-level risk factors (no prior recordings in 5 years, vacant status, unencumbered, non-resident owner). Entrust reports a 40% YoY increase in deepfake-related fraud attempts (2026), with AI-forged deeds, government IDs, and notary stamps as primary vectors in real estate title fraud. Notary commission validation is a critical check -- invalid or expired notary credentials are a high-confidence fraud indicator.

objects.name: Ghost Broker Policy Pattern — Multiple Policies with Disposable Contacts and Below-Market Premiums
objects.description: Detects ghost broker activity by identifying intermediaries submitting multiple insurance policies using disposable contact details (temporary email addresses, prepaid phone numbers) with premiums significantly below market rates. Ghost broking victims increased 93% in 2025, with organized operators selling fake or fraudulently obtained policies at 30-60% below market rates. The combination of high policy volume, rotating disposable contacts, and below-market pricing is the hallmark pattern of ghost broker operations. City of London Police made arrests in May 2025 and IFED designated February 2026 as a ghost broking intensification month.

objects.name: Ghost Portal Infrastructure Detection — Fake Insurance Verification on Recently Registered Domains
objects.description: Detects ghost portal infrastructure — fraudulent insurance verification websites deployed on recently registered domains that return valid-looking but unverifiable policy numbers. Ghost portals represent the evolution of ghost broking into a fraud-as-a-service model, where operators build and sell fake insurance verification platforms to other fraudsters. These portals are typically deployed on domains registered within the past 90 days, use insurance-related keywords, and mimic legitimate insurer verification workflows. Detection focuses on DNS queries and web traffic to recently registered domains containing insurance verification terminology.

objects.name: Chargeback Velocity Pattern — Serial Dispute Filing Across Merchants with Confirmed Delivery
objects.description: Detects friendly fraud chargeback abuse by identifying cardholders with 3 or more chargebacks filed within a 90-day window across different merchants where delivery was confirmed for the original transactions. Friendly fraud represents 36% of all fraud, with 337 million chargebacks projected for 2026 costing USD 15.3 billion in the US. Chargeback abuse surged 233% between Q1 and Q3 2025. The combination of multi-merchant dispute filing with contradicting delivery evidence is a high-confidence indicator of first-party chargeback abuse rather than legitimate disputes. Merchants lose USD 4.61 for every USD 1.00 of friendly fraud.

objects.name: First-Party Dispute Anomaly — Chargeback with Delivery Confirmation, Device Match, and No Merchant Contact
objects.description: Detects high-confidence friendly fraud by identifying chargebacks where three independent indicators contradict the dispute claim: (1) delivery was confirmed for the original order, (2) the device fingerprint filing the dispute matches the device used for the original purchase, and (3) no merchant contact was attempted before the chargeback was filed. The triple correlation of delivery evidence, device match, and merchant bypass is a strong signal that the cardholder is the original purchaser who received the goods and chose to file a chargeback rather than a legitimate return. 84% of consumers find chargebacks simpler than contacting merchants, creating systemic abuse of the dispute mechanism.

objects.name: Cookie Stuffing Detection — Affiliate Cookies Set Without Corresponding Click Events
objects.description: Detects cookie stuffing — the most prevalent affiliate fraud technique (approximately 60% of cases) — by identifying affiliates that set tracking cookies in user browsers without corresponding user click events. Cookie stuffing uses hidden iframes, 1x1 pixel images, or JavaScript injection to drop affiliate cookies without the user's knowledge or intent. This steals attribution credit from legitimate affiliates and organic traffic, inflating the fraudulent affiliate's commission payments. Detection relies on the cookie-to-click ratio: legitimate affiliates typically have a ratio near 1:1, while cookie stuffers exhibit ratios of 5:1 or higher, or set cookies with zero associated clicks entirely. Global ad fraud is projected at USD 71 billion in 2025.

objects.name: Bot Traffic Behavioral Anomaly — Mechanical Consistency in Affiliate Session Metrics
objects.description: Detects bot-generated affiliate traffic by identifying sessions with mechanical behavioral consistency — identical session durations, linear scroll patterns, and zero mouse movement variance — that indicate automated rather than human browsing. Bot networks account for approximately 40% of all click fraud, and AI-powered bots increasingly mimic individual human sessions. However, bot traffic still exhibits statistically detectable patterns at the population level: genuine human traffic has natural variance in behavioral metrics, while bot traffic — even sophisticated AI bots — produces distributions with anomalously low standard deviation. This rule analyzes session-level behavioral distributions per affiliate to detect mechanical consistency at the aggregate level.

objects.name: AI-Generated Claims Document Detection — Metadata Anomalies and Generation Tool Signatures
objects.description: Detects AI-generated or AI-altered insurance claims documents by analyzing metadata anomalies including GAN artifacts, inconsistent EXIF data, and AI generation tool signatures. An estimated 25-30% of insurance claims now involve some form of GenAI-altered content. This rule targets the document forensics layer: photos submitted without legitimate camera metadata, documents with AI tool signatures in creation metadata, images with frequency domain anomalies characteristic of GAN generation, and GPS coordinates that contradict the claimed loss location. The insurance fraud detection market is growing from USD 7.5B to USD 9.13B reflecting industry investment in these countermeasures. Debener et al. (2023) demonstrate that XGBoost and isolation forests provide complementary detection approaches for anomalous claims.

objects.name: Deepfake Vehicle Damage Photo Pattern — Pixel Artifacts, Lighting Inconsistencies, and AI Generation Indicators
objects.description: Detects deepfake vehicle damage photos in insurance claims by analyzing pixel-level artifacts, lighting and shadow inconsistencies, and metadata indicating AI image generation tools. AI-generated vehicle damage photos represent an acute threat to auto insurance claims processing, as generative AI can produce realistic collision, hail, and vandalism damage images that bypass visual inspection by claims adjusters. Detection relies on computer vision analysis: GAN-generated images exhibit characteristic pixel artifacts at damage boundaries, physically impossible lighting/shadow combinations, and frequency domain signatures distinct from camera-captured photos. This rule targets vehicle-specific claims (collision, comprehensive, vandalism) and correlates image forensics scores with claim characteristics.

objects.name: Stablecoin Flow to CEX via Hot Wallet Sweep Pattern
objects.description: Detects the 2-hop hot wallet sweep pattern used in industrialized stablecoin laundering pipelines: illicit or high-risk funds flow from a flagged/suspicious address to a centralized exchange (CEX) deposit address (hop 1), which is then automatically swept into the exchange institutional hot wallet (hop 2). Confirming both hops confirms the exchange relationship and receipt of flagged funds. This pattern was documented by ICIJ in the Huione Group investigation, where at least $408 million flowed to Binance and $226 million to OKX via TRON/USDT through this exact mechanism. The detection leverages publicly available exchange Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) address lists and Arkham Intelligence illicit wallet tags to attribute both source risk and destination exchange. TRON/USDT is the primary monitoring surface given its dominance as the SE Asian fraud compound laundering rail.

objects.name: Crypto-to-Cash Desk — Ephemeral Wallet and Unlicensed OTC Indicators
objects.description: Detects crypto-to-cash desk operations that convert USDT to physical currency with minimal or no KYC, generating fresh wallet addresses per transaction to defeat blockchain tracing. These unlicensed OTC operations represent the final monetization layer in stablecoin laundering pipelines, bridging the gap between on-chain cryptocurrency and usable physical cash. ICIJ investigators documented such operations in Dubai and Eastern European cities during the Coin Laundry investigation, with one desk processing $2 million in volume over 10 days on the TRON network alone — and critically, that desk did not appear in any major blockchain analytics provider attribution database (Chainalysis, TRM, Elliptic). The detection targets ephemeral wallets (< 7 days old, < 3 prior transactions) receiving USDT from multiple distinct sources on TRON, where the destination wallet is not attributed in any known analytics or exchange Proof-of-Reserves database.

objects.name: Shell Company Address Concentration as Fraud Infrastructure Indicator
objects.description: Detects abnormal concentration of corporate registrations at a single registered address as an indicator of shell company infrastructure used for fraud, money laundering, or beneficial ownership obfuscation. The ICIJ/OpenCorporates investigation of Wyoming documented that 40% of all Wyoming LLCs are registered to just two buildings in Sheridan, WY, with a 30% spike in LLC registrations in 2023 alone. Wyoming now surpasses Delaware in companies registered per capita. Wyoming LLC services are actively marketed in Cyprus, Singapore, and other offshore jurisdictions as tax avoidance and asset-shielding vehicles. Millions in PPP loan fraud were traced to shell companies registered at a single Wyoming storefront address. The Corporate Transparency Act beneficial ownership registry — catalyzed by the FinCEN Files investigation — was effectively gutted in 2025 when the Trump Administration suspended all enforcement and deleted previously submitted data, removing the primary countermeasure against shell company opacity in the United States. This rule targets the recon phase (P1) where fraud infrastructure is established through mass corporate registration at concentrated addresses.

objects.name: ASN Reputation Clustering — High Abuse-Density Autonomous Systems
objects.description: Detects network traffic to or from IP addresses within autonomous systems (ASNs) that exhibit high abuse density — defined as a concentration of abuse reports, malware hosting, and fraud-associated domains relative to total IP allocation. BPH operators concentrate on ASNs with high abuse-to-IP ratios due to their resistance to takedown. ASN-level reputation clustering is more resilient to infrastructure rotation than individual IP blocking, as operators rotate IPs within the same ASN. Sourced from Flare Academy BPH Webinar and Recorded Future TAE provider intelligence.

objects.name: Infrastructure Rotation Velocity — Rapid DNS IP Changes Within BPH Networks
objects.description: Detects domains exhibiting rapid IP address rotation characteristic of bulletproof hosting infrastructure management. BPH operators rotate IP addresses every 24-72 hours to evade blocklists, with emergency rotation following IOC publication. A domain resolving to 4+ unique IPs within 7 days — particularly when those IPs span multiple TAE provider ASNs — is a strong indicator of managed BPH infrastructure rotation. This detection complements static IP blocklists by identifying the rotation behavior itself. Sourced from Flare Academy BPH Webinar and Cybercrime Diaries BPH landscape analysis.

objects.name: AiTM Antibot Cloaking Detection — Divergent Content by Client Type
objects.description: Detects phishing pages that serve different content to automated scanners versus human visitors — a key evasion technique used by PhaaS platforms including Bluekit, Tycoon 2FA, and NakedPages. Antibot cloaking typically returns benign content (blank pages, Wikipedia redirects, legitimate-looking sites) to known scanner User-Agents, IP ranges associated with security vendors, and headless browsers, while serving the actual phishing page to real victims. Detection compares HTTP responses for the same URL across different client profiles. Sourced from Bluekit PhaaS TI report (CrimsonVector, March 2026).

objects.name: Browser Fingerprint Spoofing — User-Agent Inconsistency in Authentication Flow
objects.description: Detects authentication sessions where the User-Agent string changes between sequential authentication steps — a strong indicator of AiTM proxy-based session hijacking. Bluekit advertises "full 2FA support with emulation/spoofing of geolocation and browser information," and Sneaky 2FA exhibits an "impossible device shift" where Safari/iOS is used for login but Edge/Windows for session resume. When a legitimate user authenticates, the User-Agent remains consistent throughout the flow. AiTM proxies may inject different User-Agents at different stages due to proxy architecture or deliberate fingerprint spoofing. Sourced from Bluekit PhaaS TI report and Sekoia TDR Sneaky 2FA analysis.

objects.name: Crypto Laundering Service Fee Pattern — Percentage-Based Deduction on Transfers
objects.description: Detects cryptocurrency transfer patterns consistent with laundering service fee structures. Illicit crypto exchange services charge 2.8%-8.5% base fees plus a 4% "dirty funds" surcharge, resulting in outbound amounts that are consistently 93-97% of inbound amounts. When a wallet receives cryptocurrency and forwards approximately 93-97% to another address within 24 hours — retaining 3-7% as a service fee — this is a strong indicator of a crypto mixing or cashout service. The retained percentage serves as the service operator's commission. Sourced from Cybercrime Diaries undercover exchange contact research (June 2025).

objects.name: Stablecoin-to-Decentralized-Stablecoin Swap Velocity
objects.description: Detects when a wallet receives USDT/USDC and swaps to decentralized stablecoins (DAI, sDAI, LUSD, RAI) via a DEX within 24 hours, particularly when the source wallet has elevated risk scores. The IRGC's documented USDT-to-DAI shift after mid-2025 Tether freezes is the direct intelligence basis. Centralized stablecoins can be frozen by issuers; swapping to decentralized alternatives defeats this control.

objects.name: Wrapped Stablecoin Bridge Transfer from High-Risk Source
objects.description: Detects stablecoin bridge transactions where USDT/USDC is wrapped through bridge protocols to create wrapped representations (wUSDT, wUSDC) on destination chains, and the source address has elevated risk indicators or recent exposure to sanctioned addresses. Bridging defeats the original issuer's freeze capability on the destination chain, making this a key laundering technique for sanctioned actors.

objects.name: Rapid Wallet Fan-Out Exceeding 100 Wallets Post-Theft
objects.description: Detects when a single wallet or cluster distributes funds across 100+ new wallets within 48 hours following a large-value transfer (>$1M). Directly models the DPRK Bybit laundering pattern where PRESSURE CHOLLIMA distributed stolen funds across 125,000+ Ethereum wallets. Existing DL-0196 and DL-0197 cover CEX off-ramp detection; this rule covers the upstream distancing and layering phase.

objects.name: Micro-Splitting Stablecoin Donations to Rotating Wallets
objects.description: Detect patterns of small-value stablecoin transfers ($10-$500) sent to wallets that are used only once or twice before rotating to new addresses. Models the ISIL/Al-Qaeda donation solicitation pattern: rotating wallet addresses, micro-splitting, and multi-hop transfers designed to evade transaction monitoring thresholds.

objects.name: New gTLD Domain Registration Burst with Phishing Characteristics
objects.description: Detect bulk domain registrations (5+ in 24h from same registrant/nameserver) on high-abuse gTLDs (.TOP, .BOND, .XYZ, .SHOP, .XIN, .CFD, .LOL) with brand-keyword presence, domain age < 7 days, and low registration cost. Interisle found 37% of phishing domains were bulk-registered and new gTLDs accounted for 51% of all phishing domains.

objects.name: Legitimate PaaS Subdomain Hosting Phishing Content
objects.description: Detect URLs hosted on known PaaS free subdomain services (*.pages.dev, *.webflow.io, *.vercel.app, *.github.io, *.gitbook.io, *.workers.dev, *.r2.dev) that contain financial brand keywords or trigger phishing heuristics. These subdomains inherit the PaaS provider's domain reputation, bypassing domain-age and reputation filters commonly used in fraud detection.

objects.name: IDN Homograph Domain Targeting Crypto Brands
objects.description: Detect DNS queries or URL accesses to internationalized domain names (IDN/punycode with xn-- prefix) that visually resemble crypto brand domains (bitpay, coinbase, metamask, phantom, pancakeswap, uniswap, etc.). Interisle documented 2,655 IDN homograph phishing domains with significant crypto brand targeting.

objects.name: Fake CAPTCHA Campaign Redirect Chain Detection
objects.description: Detect web access patterns consistent with fake CAPTCHA campaigns: user visits a page with CAPTCHA verification UI, is instructed to copy/execute clipboard content (PowerShell, cmd, mshta), which triggers malware or stealer download. CrowdStrike documented a +563% increase in fake CAPTCHA campaigns in 2025. Used by BRASH SPIDER (Doshell Stealer) and COOKIE SPIDER (SHAMOS).
